papers.title: Add-on versus switch to peginterferon in nucleos(t)ide analogue-treated chronic hepatitis B
papers.abstract: This project contains the analysis dataset and code that reproduce the network meta-analysis reported in: **Chu X, Wang Y, Dai L, Wang L, Liu G, Ji G. Add-on versus switch to peginterferon in nucleos(t)ide analogue-treated chronic hepatitis B: a network meta-analysis weighing efficacy against virologic rebound.** The study compares add-on and switch-to peginterferon strategies against continued nucleos(t)ide analogue monotherapy in patients with chronic hepatitis B, using a frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis of 14 randomised controlled trials (1,640 patients in the network). All data were extracted from published trial reports; no individual patient data are included. ## Contents - `nma_data.csv` — per-arm extracted outcome data for the 14 included trials - `nma_analysis.R` — main network meta-analysis of HBsAg clearance (league table, network plot, forest plots, P-scores, node-splitting, net heat plot, sensitivity analysis excluding He 2016) - `funnel_v10.R` — comparison-adjusted funnel plot (Fig. S4) - `review_r1r2.R` — study-level meta-regressions (treatment duration, baseline HBsAg, NA duration, PEG-IFN type, HBeAg-positive proportion) and last-follow-up sensitivity analyses (ARES long-term follow-up; Al Ashgar 2017) - `ga_graphical_abstract.py` — graphical abstract figure (Python/matplotlib) - `README.txt` — variable definitions and running instructions

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on the comparison of add-on versus switch to peginterferon strategies in patients with chronic hepatitis B who are already receiving nucleos(t)ide analogue treatment. The central question is whether these strategies differ in efficacy and virologic rebound when compared to continued nucleos(t)ide analogue monotherapy.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review employs a frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis of 14 randomised controlled trials involving 1,640 patients. All data were extracted from published trial reports, and no individual patient data are included. The analysis includes a league table, network plot, forest plots, P-scores, node-splitting, net heat plot, and sensitivity analysis excluding He 2016.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The network meta-analysis compares add-on and switch-to peginterferon strategies against continued nucleos(t)ide analogue monotherapy in patients with chronic hepatitis B. The study provides a comprehensive evaluation of efficacy and virologic rebound, with results and conclusions derived from the analysis of these trials.

papers.source_body_en: This project contains the analysis dataset and code that reproduce the network meta-analysis reported in: **Chu X, Wang Y, Dai L, Wang L, Liu G, Ji G. Add-on versus switch to peginterferon in nucleos(t)ide analogue-treated chronic hepatitis B: a network meta-analysis weighing efficacy against virologic rebound.** The study compares add-on and switch-to peginterferon strategies against continued nucleos(t)ide analogue monotherapy in patients with chronic hepatitis B, using a frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis of 14 randomised controlled trials (1,640 patients in the network). All data were extracted from published trial reports; no individual patient data are included. ## Contents - `nma_data.csv` — per-arm extracted outcome data for the 14 included trials - `nma_analysis.R` — main network meta-analysis of HBsAg clearance (league table, network plot, forest plots, P-scores, node-splitting, net heat plot, sensitivity analysis excluding He 2016) - `funnel_v10.R` — comparison-adjusted funnel plot (Fig. S4) - `review_r1r2.R` — study-level meta-regressions (treatment duration, baseline HBsAg, NA duration, PEG-IFN type, HBeAg-positive proportion) and last-follow-up sensitivity analyses (ARES long-term follow-up; Al Ashgar 2017) - `ga_graphical_abstract.py` — graphical abstract figure (Python/matplotlib) - `README.txt` — variable definitions and running instructions

papers.title: HBV exposure, HBsAg positivity, and anti-HDV seroprevalence in rural communities along the Iran–Afghanistan border: a community-based cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) exposure and hepatitis D virus (HDV) antibody prevalence remain incompletely characterized in rural eastern Iran. We estimated anti-HBc seroprevalence, conditional HBsAg positivity, and anti-HDV seropositivity in three border villages. We conducted a community-based cross-sectional serosurvey with census-targeted recruitment in three villages of Nehbandan County, South Khorasan Province, Iran, during May–June 2024. All evaluable specimens were tested for total anti-HBc. HBsAg was measured only in anti-HBc-positive specimens, and anti-HDV was measured among participants with a final HBsAg-positive classification. Correlates of anti-HBc positivity were estimated using Firth penalized logistic regression. Of 842 residents, 494 participated (58.7%), and 489 had an evaluable anti-HBc result. Anti-HBc seroprevalence was 23.3% (114/489; 95% CI 19.6%–27.3%), including 5.3% at age ≤ 30 years and 45.3% at age > 30 years. In the primary model, age > 30 years (adjusted OR 19.36, 95% CI 10.34–38.89), Khvajeh Monji Kuh residence (4.50, 2.46–8.46), and family history of HBV (2.52, 1.12–5.62) were associated with anti-HBc positivity. The family-history confidence interval included 1 after adding education and occupation. Among anti-HBc-positive participants, 42/114 (36.8%, exact 95% CI 28.0%–46.4%) were HBsAg positive. Anti-HDV seropositivity was 5/41 (12.2%, 4.1%–26.2%). Fifteen HBsAg-positive participants initiated treatment after specialist assessment. HBV exposure was concentrated among older participants. Village comparisons were descriptive because participation differed substantially, and family-history estimates were sensitive to model specification. Birth-cohort analyses did not establish an additional cohort association beyond flexible adjustment for attained age.Staged testing prevented estimation of population HBsAg prevalence. Anti-HDV seropositivity supports antibody screening followed by HDV RNA testing to establish active infection.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to characterize HBV exposure and anti-HDV seroprevalence in rural communities along the Iran–Afghanistan border. A community-based cross-sectional serosurvey was conducted in three villages of Nehbandan County, South Khorasan Province, Iran, during May–June 2024, with census-targeted recruitment. Anti-HBc seroprevalence was 23.3% (95% CI 19.6%–27.3%), with higher rates observed in participants over 30 years old. However, village comparisons were limited due to differing participation rates, and family-history estimates were sensitive to model specification. These findings highlight the need for targeted screening and further research to address HBV-related health concerns in these communities.

papers.source_body_en: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) exposure and hepatitis D virus (HDV) antibody prevalence remain incompletely characterized in rural eastern Iran. We estimated anti-HBc seroprevalence, conditional HBsAg positivity, and anti-HDV seropositivity in three border villages. We conducted a community-based cross-sectional serosurvey with census-targeted recruitment in three villages of Nehbandan County, South Khorasan Province, Iran, during May–June 2024. All evaluable specimens were tested for total anti-HBc. HBsAg was measured only in anti-HBc-positive specimens, and anti-HDV was measured among participants with a final HBsAg-positive classification. Correlates of anti-HBc positivity were estimated using Firth penalized logistic regression. Of 842 residents, 494 participated (58.7%), and 489 had an evaluable anti-HBc result. Anti-HBc seroprevalence was 23.3% (114/489; 95% CI 19.6%–27.3%), including 5.3% at age ≤ 30 years and 45.3% at age > 30 years. In the primary model, age > 30 years (adjusted OR 19.36, 95% CI 10.34–38.89), Khvajeh Monji Kuh residence (4.50, 2.46–8.46), and family history of HBV (2.52, 1.12–5.62) were associated with anti-HBc positivity. The family-history confidence interval included 1 after adding education and occupation. Among anti-HBc-positive participants, 42/114 (36.8%, exact 95% CI 28.0%–46.4%) were HBsAg positive. Anti-HDV seropositivity was 5/41 (12.2%, 4.1%–26.2%). Fifteen HBsAg-positive participants initiated treatment after specialist assessment. HBV exposure was concentrated among older participants. Village comparisons were descriptive because participation differed substantially, and family-history estimates were sensitive to model specification. Birth-cohort analyses did not establish an additional cohort association beyond flexible adjustment for attained age.Staged testing prevented estimation of population HBsAg prevalence. Anti-HDV seropositivity supports antibody screening followed by HDV RNA testing to establish active infection.

papers.full_text: ABSTRACTVaccination is the primary strategy for preventing hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, but its frequency remains insufficiently characterized among cancer patients. This study evaluated the regional distribution of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city, Brazil. We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients who underwent hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) serological testing at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) in 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity was defined as reactive anti-HBs and non-reactive hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc). Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were performed to identify associated factors. Among 1,143 patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, 60.6% self-identified White, and 76.8% had solid tumors. Overall, 26.2% of cancer patients had serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the North Zone had a lower frequency than the South Zone (20.7% versus 28.9%), although regional differences were not statistically significant after multivariable adjustment. Female sex (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.23-2.27, p = 0.001) and younger age (18-39 years versus ≥ 60 years: aPR = 6.89, 95% CI: 4.72-10.95, p < 0.001) were independently associated with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. These findings indicate a low frequency of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients across Sao Paulo, particularly among older adults and men. MATERIALS AND METHODSStudy designThis retrospective observational study included adult cancer patients receiving care at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP), affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (HCFMUSP), between January and December 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B, defined as immunity resulting from prior hepatitis B vaccination rather than previous infection, was considered present when anti-HBs was reactive and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) was non-reactive. All serological tests were performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) on the Alinity i system (Abbott Diagnostics, Chicago, IL, USA) at the Central Laboratory Division of HCFMUSP. According to the laboratory’s routine procedures, an anti-HBs titer ≥ 10 IU/L was classified as reactive. Testing was conducted as part of routine clinical care before the study began, with data subsequently retrieved from the hospital’s medical records.EthicsThis study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Analysis of Research Projects of the HCFMUSP under protocols No 6.120.828 and 6.718.762 (CAAE: 70101521.9.0000.0068). Requirement for informed consent was waived, and all data were de-identified before analysis to ensure patient confidentiality.Data sourcePatients with solid tumors or hematologic malignancies who attended the ICESP, aged 18 years or older and who underwent anti-HBs serological testing were eligible for inclusion. Patients without anti-HBc testing or with reactive anti-HBc or hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) results were excluded, as were those who did not reside in Sao Paulo city. All eligible patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria during the study period (January to December 2023) were consecutively identified and included; therefore, no sampling strategy was applied.Demographic characteristics (i.e., age, sex [sex assigned at birth], and ethnicity/skin color), primary cancer type (i.e., solid tumors or hematological malignancies), and residential zone within Sao Paulo city were retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. Ethnicity/skin color was classified according to participants’ self-identification using the Brazilian census classification system: Brazilians of African origin who self-identified as “Black,” Indigenous Brazilians who self-identified as “Indigenous,” Brazilians of mixed ethnic background who self-identified as “Pardo” (“Brown/Mixed-ethnicity”), Brazilians of European origin who self-identified as “White,” and Brazilians of Asian origin who self-identified as “Asian.”Statistical analysisAge was analyzed both as a continuous variable and as a categorical variable (18-39, 40-59, and ≥ 60 years). Sex was classified as male or female; ethnicity/skin color as White or non-White (including Black, Indigenous, Pardo, and Asian); and primary cancer type as hematological malignancies or solid tumors.Associations between zone of residence (Central, East, North, West, and South), epidemiological characteristics, and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B (anti-HBs) were evaluated by using univariable Poisson regression to estimate unadjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Consistent with established variable-selection procedures, variables with p-values < 0.20 in the univariable analyses were selected for inclusion in the multivariable Poisson regression model. Differences in demographic characteristics and cancer type across the five zones were assessed using Pearson’s chi-square test. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Study designThis retrospective observational study included adult cancer patients receiving care at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP), affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (HCFMUSP), between January and December 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B, defined as immunity resulting from prior hepatitis B vaccination rather than previous infection, was considered present when anti-HBs was reactive and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) was non-reactive. All serological tests were performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) on the Alinity i system (Abbott Diagnostics, Chicago, IL, USA) at the Central Laboratory Division of HCFMUSP. According to the laboratory’s routine procedures, an anti-HBs titer ≥ 10 IU/L was classified as reactive. Testing was conducted as part of routine clinical care before the study began, with data subsequently retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. Supplementary MaterialSupplementary information are available at https://www.scielo.br/10.48331/SCIELODATA.EOBWJF Supplementary PDF RESULTSIn 2023, 2,792 adult cancer patients underwent anti-HBs serological testing at ICESP. Of these, 327 were excluded because anti-HBc testing had not been performed, 253 because they were anti-HBc-reactive, and 33 because they were HBsAg-reactive. Although 2,179 patients met the initial serological criteria, 1,036 were excluded because they resided outside Sao Paulo city. Consequently, the final study population comprised 1,143 patients who met all inclusion and exclusion criteria.Among included patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, and 60.6% self-identified as White. Solid tumors accounted for 76.8% of cases, whereas hematological malignancies accounted for 19.4%. Patients were distributed across all zones of the city, with the largest proportions residing in the South (29.7%) and East (25.0%) (Supplementary Table S1).Overall, 26.2% (299/1,143) of cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city showed serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the highest proportions were observed in the South (28.9%, 98/339) and East (28.7%, 82/286), whereas the lowest was observed in the North (20.7%, 51/246). The regional distribution and corresponding 95% CI are presented in Figure 1.In the univariable Poisson regression, serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B was less frequently observed among patients residing in the North than those residing in the South (20.7% versus 28.9%; PR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.51-1.01, p = 0.054).However, this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for potential confounders in the multivariable Poisson model (p = 0.139), indicating no independent association between zone of residence and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. In contrast, age group and sex remained independently associated with the outcome (p < 0.05) (Table 1). Compared with patients aged ≥ 60 years, those aged 18-39 years were more likely to present serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity (adjusted PR [aPR] = 3.56, 95% CI: 2.66-4.77), whereas patients aged 40-59 years were also more likely to present the outcome (aPR = 1.73, 95% CI: 1.30-2.31). Likewise, female patients were more likely than male patients to present serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity (aPR = 1.42, 95% CI: 1.10-1.82).No statistically significant differences were observed in the distribution of age (p = 0.184), sex (p = 0.504), ethnicity/skin color (p = 0.835), or primary cancer type (p = 0.340) across the five zones of Sao Paulo city (Table 2). Descriptively, the West had the highest proportion of younger adults (18-39 years, 20.5%), whereas the North had the highest proportion of older adults (≥ 60 years, 55.3%). Female patients, White patients, and patients with solid tumors predominated across all regions. Likewise, despite slight descriptive variation in the proportion of patients with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B across the five zones (Figure 1), no statistically significant regional differences were observed (p = 0.180). full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTVaccination is the primary strategy for preventing hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, but its frequency remains insufficiently characterized among cancer patients. This study evaluated the regional distribution of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city, Brazil. We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients who underwent hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) serological testing at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) in 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity was defined as reactive anti-HBs and non-reactive hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc). Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were performed to identify associated factors. Among 1,143 patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, 60.6% self-identified White, and 76.8% had solid tumors. Overall, 26.2% of cancer patients had serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the North Zone had a lower frequency than the South Zone (20.7% versus 28.9%), although regional differences were not statistically significant after multivariable adjustment. Female sex (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.23-2.27, p = 0.001) and younger age (18-39 years versus ≥ 60 years: aPR = 6.89, 95% CI: 4.72-10.95, p < 0.001) were independently associated with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. These findings indicate a low frequency of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients across Sao Paulo, particularly among older adults and men.
full_text_sections.methods: MATERIALS AND METHODSStudy designThis retrospective observational study included adult cancer patients receiving care at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP), affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (HCFMUSP), between January and December 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B, defined as immunity resulting from prior hepatitis B vaccination rather than previous infection, was considered present when anti-HBs was reactive and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) was non-reactive. All serological tests were performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) on the Alinity i system (Abbott Diagnostics, Chicago, IL, USA) at the Central Laboratory Division of HCFMUSP. According to the laboratory’s routine procedures, an anti-HBs titer ≥ 10 IU/L was classified as reactive. Testing was conducted as part of routine clinical care before the study began, with data subsequently retrieved from the hospital’s medical records.EthicsThis study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Analysis of Research Projects of the HCFMUSP under protocols No 6.120.828 and 6.718.762 (CAAE: 70101521.9.0000.0068). Requirement for informed consent was waived, and all data were de-identified before analysis to ensure patient confidentiality.Data sourcePatients with solid tumors or hematologic malignancies who attended the ICESP, aged 18 years or older and who underwent anti-HBs serological testing were eligible for inclusion. Patients without anti-HBc testing or with reactive anti-HBc or hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) results were excluded, as were those who did not reside in Sao Paulo city. All eligible patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria during the study period (January to December 2023) were consecutively identified and included; therefore, no sampling strategy was applied.Demographic characteristics (i.e., age, sex [sex assigned at birth], and ethnicity/skin color), primary cancer type (i.e., solid tumors or hematological malignancies), and residential zone within Sao Paulo city were retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. Ethnicity/skin color was classified according to participants’ self-identification using the Brazilian census classification system: Brazilians of African origin who self-identified as “Black,” Indigenous Brazilians who self-identified as “Indigenous,” Brazilians of mixed ethnic background who self-identified as “Pardo” (“Brown/Mixed-ethnicity”), Brazilians of European origin who self-identified as “White,” and Brazilians of Asian origin who self-identified as “Asian.”Statistical analysisAge was analyzed both as a continuous variable and as a categorical variable (18-39, 40-59, and ≥ 60 years). Sex was classified as male or female; ethnicity/skin color as White or non-White (including Black, Indigenous, Pardo, and Asian); and primary cancer type as hematological malignancies or solid tumors.Associations between zone of residence (Central, East, North, West, and South), epidemiological characteristics, and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B (anti-HBs) were evaluated by using univariable Poisson regression to estimate unadjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Consistent with established variable-selection procedures, variables with p-values < 0.20 in the univariable analyses were selected for inclusion in the multivariable Poisson regression model. Differences in demographic characteristics and cancer type across the five zones were assessed using Pearson’s chi-square test. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B, defined as immunity resulting from prior hepatitis B vaccination rather than previous infection, was considered present when anti-HBs was reactive and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) was non-reactive. All serological tests were performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) on the Alinity i system (Abbott Diagnostics, Chicago, IL, USA) at the Central Laboratory Division of HCFMUSP. According to the laboratory’s routine procedures, an anti-HBs titer ≥ 10 IU/L was classified as reactive. Testing was conducted as part of routine clinical care before the study began, with data subsequently retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. full_text_sections.results: RESULTSIn 2023, 2,792 adult cancer patients underwent anti-HBs serological testing at ICESP. Of these, 327 were excluded because anti-HBc testing had not been performed, 253 because they were anti-HBc-reactive, and 33 because they were HBsAg-reactive. Although 2,179 patients met the initial serological criteria, 1,036 were excluded because they resided outside Sao Paulo city. Consequently, the final study population comprised 1,143 patients who met all inclusion and exclusion criteria.Among included patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, and 60.6% self-identified as White. Solid tumors accounted for 76.8% of cases, whereas hematological malignancies accounted for 19.4%. Patients were distributed across all zones of the city, with the largest proportions residing in the South (29.7%) and East (25.0%) (Supplementary Table S1).Overall, 26.2% (299/1,143) of cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city showed serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the highest proportions were observed in the South (28.9%, 98/339) and East (28.7%, 82/286), whereas the lowest was observed in the North (20.7%, 51/246). The regional distribution and corresponding 95% CI are presented in Figure 1.In the univariable Poisson regression, serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B was less frequently observed among patients residing in the North than those residing in the South (20.7% versus 28.9%; PR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.51-1.01, p = 0.054).However, this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for potential confounders in the multivariable Poisson model (p = 0.139), indicating no independent association between zone of residence and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. In contrast, age group and sex remained independently associated with the outcome (p < 0.05) (Table 1). Compared with patients aged ≥ 60 years, those aged 18-39 years were more likely to present serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity (adjusted PR [aPR] = 3.56, 95% CI: 2.66-4.77), whereas patients aged 40-59 years were also more likely to present the outcome (aPR = 1.73, 95% CI: 1.30-2.31). Likewise, female patients were more likely than male patients to present serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity (aPR = 1.42, 95% CI: 1.10-1.82).No statistically significant differences were observed in the distribution of age (p = 0.184), sex (p = 0.504), ethnicity/skin color (p = 0.835), or primary cancer type (p = 0.340) across the five zones of Sao Paulo city (Table 2). Descriptively, the West had the highest proportion of younger adults (18-39 years, 20.5%), whereas the North had the highest proportion of older adults (≥ 60 years, 55.3%). Female patients, White patients, and patients with solid tumors predominated across all regions. Likewise, despite slight descriptive variation in the proportion of patients with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B across the five zones (Figure 1), no statistically significant regional differences were observed (p = 0.180). Previous Brazilian studies have similarly reported detectable anti-HBs in only 68.5% of vaccinated medical students 11 and 38.9% of children aged 1-15 years 12 , despite completion of the three-dose vaccination schedule. Furthermore, childhood hepatitis B vaccination coverage in Brazil was only 55.3% in 2021, remaining below the national target established by the Ministry of Health 13 .Sex-related differences were also observed. full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONOnly 26.2% of cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city presented serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Although regional differences were not statistically significant after adjustment, older adults and men were less likely to have serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. These findings support the need to strengthen HBV screening and vaccination assessment in oncology care.
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONGlobally, an estimated 0.9 million individuals were newly infected with hepatitis B virus (HBV) in 2024. From 2000 to 2024, Brazil reported 302,351 newly diagnosed cases of hepatitis B, of which 63,670 occurred in Sao Paulo State 1 . Concurrently, Brazil recorded an estimated 627,193 new cancer cases in 2022 2 . Within this context, preventive strategies are critical for patients with cancer, who are at increased risk of HBV reactivation and other infection-related complications driven by disease- and treatment-related immunosuppression 3 . In particular, anticancer therapies may predispose patients with previous HBV infection to viral reactivation and severe hepatic complications 3 .Vaccination against HBV is the primary strategy for preventing HBV infection in both the general population and patients receiving anticancer therapy. In the general population, seroprotection rates after completion of the full vaccination schedule are expected to reach 98%-100% in children and 90%-95% in adults. However, vaccine-induced immune responses are less robust among individuals older than 40-50 years 4 . The isolated presence of hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs), in the absence of anti-HBc, is widely accepted as serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Therefore, this study aims to determine the frequency and regional distribution of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city. EthicsThis study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Analysis of Research Projects of the HCFMUSP under protocols No 6.120.828 and 6.718.762 (CAAE: 70101521.9.0000.0068). Requirement for informed consent was waived, and all data were de-identified before analysis to ensure patient confidentiality. Patients without anti-HBc testing or with reactive anti-HBc or hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) results were excluded, as were those who did not reside in Sao Paulo city. Ethnicity/skin color was classified according to participants’ self-identification using the Brazilian census classification system: Brazilians of African origin who self-identified as “Black,” Indigenous Brazilians who self-identified as “Indigenous,” Brazilians of mixed ethnic background who self-identified as “Pardo” (“Brown/Mixed-ethnicity”), Brazilians of European origin who self-identified as “White,” and Brazilians of Asian origin who self-identified as “Asian.” Statistical analysisAge was analyzed both as a continuous variable and as a categorical variable (18-39, 40-59, and ≥ 60 years). Sex was classified as male or female; ethnicity/skin color as White or non-White (including Black, Indigenous, Pardo, and Asian); and primary cancer type as hematological malignancies or solid tumors.Associations between zone of residence (Central, East, North, West, and South), epidemiological characteristics, and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B (anti-HBs) were evaluated by using univariable Poisson regression to estimate unadjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Consistent with established variable-selection procedures, variables with p-values < 0.20 in the univariable analyses were selected for inclusion in the multivariable Poisson regression model. Differences in demographic characteristics and cancer type across the five zones were assessed using Pearson’s chi-square test. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. First, given the retrospective design, selection bias cannot be ruled out because information on the anti-HBs testing strategy was unavailable, and inclusion was restricted to patients with available HBV serological results. Second, information on socioeconomic and structural determinants was unavailable. Third, ethnicity/skin color was analyzed as a dichotomous variable (White versus non-White) because of the small number of participants in specific categories, which may have masked differences among individual racial and ethnic groups. Finally, information regarding the timing of anti-HBs testing in relation to cancer diagnosis and anticancer treatment was unavailable. Therefore, it was not possible to distinguish whether low or undetectable anti-HBs levels reflected lack of vaccination, waning antibody levels over time, impaired vaccine response, treatment-related immunosuppression, or a combination of these mechanisms. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the regional distribution of serological evidence of vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients in a city in southeastern Brazil, addressing the need to understand how immunity varies across different geographic areas and populations.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study was conducted among 1,143 adult cancer patients who underwent hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) testing at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) in 2023. The population included patients with solid tumors and hematological malignancies, with demographic and clinical characteristics retrieved from medical records.
analysis.methods: Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were used to identify associated factors, with variables selected based on p-values < 0.20 in univariable analyses. Associations between zone of residence and serological evidence were evaluated using Poisson regression to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
analysis.main_results: Overall, 26.2% (299/1,143) of cancer patients showed serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. The distribution across zones was not statistically significant after adjustment for confounders, with no independent association found between zone of residence and anti-HBs status.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the regional distribution of vaccine-induced immunity did not show a significant association with zone of residence after adjusting for potential confounders, highlighting the need for targeted vaccination efforts in specific age groups.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that age-related differences in immunity to hepatitis B are significant, and may inform public health strategies to improve vaccination coverage in high-risk populations, particularly younger adults.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and potential confounding factors, but the evidence is strong due to the use of multivariable Poisson regression and a large sample size, with a moderate confidence assessment based on the statistical methods employed.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the regional distribution of serological evidence of vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients in a city in southeastern Brazil. A retrospective observational study of 1,143 patients was conducted, with data collected from medical records. Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were used to assess associations between zone of residence and immunity status. Overall, 26.2% of patients showed serological evidence of immunity, but no independent association with geographic region was found after adjustment. Age-related differences were observed, with younger adults more likely to have immunity. The study highlights the importance of targeted vaccination efforts, particularly in younger populations, to address disparities in hepatitis B immunity. The evidence is strong due to the statistical methods used, but the observational design limits causal conclusions.

papers.full_text: Abstract The current study presents a hybrid framework combining deep learning and ensemble learning models to predict hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) based on sequence variants of the hepatitis B virus (HBV)-X gene. In contrast to traditional single-model approaches, the proposed framework integrates deep learning architectures with data balancing and ensemble learning strategies to enhance predictive robustness and generalization. The dataset comprises 3,360 distinct DNA sequences categorized into HCC and Non-HCC classes, with a significant class imbalance favoring the Non-HCC group. To address this issue, the Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) was applied to reduce classification bias and improve minority class learning. Two sequence encoding strategies, One-Hot encoding and K-mer encoding (K = 3 and K = 6), were employed to capture nucleotide composition and sequence dependencies. A range of machine learning models, including Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB), Support Vector Classifier (SVC), Nu-Support Vector Classifier (NuSVC), Logistic Regression (LR), XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), and AdaBoost, as well as deep learning models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM), were systematically evaluated. To further enhance predictive performance, a hybrid stacking ensemble framework was developed, integrating a CNN–BiLSTM architecture and Random Forest as base learners, with Logistic Regression serving as the meta-classifier to combine their predictions. All methodological steps, model configurations, and evaluation strategies were explicitly defined to ensure reproducibility and facilitate verification. The proposed hybrid stacking ensemble model demonstrated superior performance compared to individual machine learning and deep learning models. One-Hot encoding consistently outperformed K-mer encoding across most models. The best-performing hybrid stacking ensemble achieved an accuracy of 0.9139 and an F1-score of 0.9126, indicating a strong balance between classification performance and generalization. The application of SMOTE further improved model stability and reduced classification bias. These results highlight that the integration of hybrid deep learning models with ensemble learning and class imbalance correction provides a significant improvement over conventional single-model approaches for HBV-related HCC prediction. The proposed framework has potential applications in clinical diagnostic systems for early and accurate detection of HCC. Future work will focus on external validation using independent datasets and further optimization of encoding strategies and advanced deep learning architectures. elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在利用 乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV)-X 基因的序列变异开发肝细胞癌 (HCC) 的预测框架,以满足改进 HBV 相关 HCC 检测诊断工具的需求。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及 3,360 个不同 DNA 序列的数据集,分为 HCC 和非 HCC 类别,其中明显的类别不平衡有利于非 HCC 组。该框架旨在通过深度学习和集成学习策略的集成来增强预测的鲁棒性和泛化性。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究评估了一系列机器学习模型,包括多项式朴素贝叶斯 (MNB)、支持 媒介 分类器 (SVC)、Nu-Support 媒介 分类器 (NuSVC)、逻辑回归 (LR)、XGBoost、随机森林 (RF) 和 AdaBoost,以及卷积神经网络 (CNN) 和双向长短期记忆 (BiLSTM) 等深度学习模型。开发了一个混合堆叠集成框架,集成了 CNN-BiLSTM 架构和随机森林作为基础学习器,逻辑回归作为元分类器来组合它们的预测。使用 One-Hot 编码和 K-mer 编码(K = 3 和 K = 6)处理数据集,以捕获核苷酸组成和序列依赖性。
elements_zh.main_results: 与单独的机器学习和深度学习模型相比,混合堆叠集成模型表现出了卓越的性能。在大多数模型中,One-Hot 编码的性能始终优于 K-mer 编码。表现最好的混合堆叠集成实现了 0.9139 的准确率和 0.9126 的 F1 分数,表明分类性能和泛化之间的强大平衡。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将结果解释为,与传统的单一模型方法相比,混合深度学习模型与集成学习和类别不平衡校​​正的集成显着改善了 HBV-X 基因序列变异的 HCC 预测。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,所提出的框架可以应用于临床诊断系统,以早期、准确地检测乙型肝炎病毒相关的肝细胞癌,从而通过改进筛查和干预策略来潜在地改善公共卫生结果。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的结果基于单个数据集,需要使用独立数据集进行外部验证以确认普遍性。证据是强有力的,因为所有方法步骤、模型配置和评估策略都被明确定义。

Researchers at the University of São Paulo examined nearly 29,000 adult cancer patients treated at a major quaternary oncology center between 2010 and 2023 and found that the proportion carrying antibodies indicating past or present HBV infection dropped from 16.5 percent to 9.9 percent over the study period. The decline, reported in the journal Cancer Causes & Control, is encouraging evidence that vaccination and changing screening practices are reshaping the viral landscape faced by oncologists. Yet the same data reveal stubborn gaps: men, older adults, and non-White patients continue to bear a disproportionate burden of previous HBV exposure, and a substantial share of admitted cancer patients were never tested at all. The clinical stakes of this epidemiology are considerable. Hepatitis B virus infects hepatocytes and can establish a chronic infection that progresses to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; infection is recognized as one of the strongest risk factors for liver cancer, raising the odds of that malignancy by roughly 47-fold. Globally, an estimated 240 million people live with chronic HBV infection. For cancer patients, the virus carries an additional threat: systemic anticancer therapies suppress immune function, which can permit viral replication to resume even in patients whose infection appeared resolved. This reactivation is driven by covalently closed circular DNA, a persistent viral reservoir that remains within the nucleus of hepatocytes long after serological recovery. A recent global meta-analysis estimated reactivation rates of approximately 10 percent among patients with hematological malignancies and 5 percent among those with solid tumors. Reactivation is not a benign event. It can force interruption, delay, or modification of cancer treatment precisely when therapy is most needed, and it may culminate in acute hepatitis, liver failure, and death. For this reason, international guidelines recommend screening for HBV before patients begin chemotherapy or other immunosuppressive regimens. Patients who test positive for the hepatitis B surface antigen should receive antiviral therapy with agents such as entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, or tenofovir alafenamide, while those who are surface-antigen negative but positive for antibody against the core antigen, known as anti-HBc, should be considered at risk of reactivation and managed with antiviral prophylaxis or serological and molecular monitoring. Despite these recommendations, screening remains inconsistently implemented across oncology centers worldwide. The São Paulo study drew on laboratory records from the São Paulo State Cancer Institute, affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the university’s Faculty of Medicine, which has treated more than 140,000 cancer patients since opening in 2008. Of 125,985 patients admitted between 2010 and 2023, 28,869, or 22.9 percent, underwent anti-HBc testing. The mean age of those tested was 56 years, roughly two-thirds were women, and 61.4 percent self-identified as White. Solid tumors accounted for 71.2 percent of the cohort, with breast cancer the most common diagnosis, while hematological malignancies made up 22.2 percent, led by non-Hodgkin lymphoma and multiple myeloma. HBV exposure was defined as anti-HBc positivity, a marker that indicates prior contact with the virus but does not by itself distinguish resolved infection from active disease. The headline finding is a statistically significant downward trend in seroprevalence, from 16.5 percent in 2010 to 9.9 percent in 2023. The decline was broad but uneven. Among men, seroprevalence fell from 25.1 percent to 12.3 percent, a steeper drop than among women, whose rates fell from 11.4 percent to 8.3 percent. Every age group improved, including patients aged 18 to 39, whose seroprevalence fell from 7.7 percent to 2.4 percent, and those aged 60 and older, whose rates declined from 20.1 percent to 13.7 percent. Seroprevalence also fell significantly among White patients and among those with solid tumors. By contrast, no significant trend emerged among non-White individuals, whose rates moved only from 21.4 percent to 17.7 percent, or among patients with hematological malignancies, whose rates remained essentially flat at around 13 percent. Multivariable logistic regression sharpened the demographic picture. Patients aged 60 or older had 4.4-fold higher odds of HBV exposure than those under 40, men had 89 percent higher odds than women, and non-White patients had 25 percent higher odds than White patients. The age gradient likely reflects cumulative lifetime exposure in cohorts born before universal neonatal vaccination, compounded by the reduced immunogenicity of hepatitis B vaccines in older adults. The sex difference may have biological underpinnings: androgens exert immunosuppressive effects, while estrogens appear to enhance immune and vaccine responses, potentially leaving men less able to clear or control the virus. The ethnic disparity points toward inequities in social determinants of health, including unequal access to vaccination, diagnosis, and treatment, a pattern consistent with prior Brazilian and international studies. Cancer type itself was not independently associated with exposure, but subgroup patterns were striking. Among hematological malignancies, non-Hodgkin lymphoma showed a seroprevalence of 15.5 percent, a malignancy repeatedly linked to HBV in meta-analyses, though the mechanisms remain unresolved. Among solid tumors, the highest rates appeared in sarcoma, at 43.5 percent, a figure the authors caution may be inflated by small numbers, and in liver and bile duct cancers, at 31.2 percent. In adjusted analyses, liver and bile duct cancers carried more than threefold higher odds of HBV exposure, and gastrointestinal cancers carried 41 percent higher odds, findings consistent with the established oncogenic role of the virus, which operates through chronic hepatic inflammation, integration of viral DNA into the host genome, and the activity of viral proteins such as HBx. Within the anti-HBc-positive group, additional testing of subsets clarified the virological picture. The hepatitis B surface antigen was positive in 7.8 percent of those tested, indicating current infection, while 73.2 percent carried anti-HBs antibodies consistent with resolved infection. Among 484 patients who underwent HBV DNA testing, 25.6 percent had detectable viral load. Taken together, most anti-HBc-positive patients showed evidence of past exposure, but a meaningful minority carried molecular or serological signs of active infection, underscoring why confirmatory testing matters before immunosuppressive therapy begins. One encouraging operational trend accompanied the epidemiological one: the proportion of admitted patients screened for anti-HBc rose from 11.1 percent in 2010 to 29.2 percent in 2023. Even so, more than two-thirds of cancer patients admitted over the period were never tested, and global data suggest screening before chemotherapy reached only about 57 percent in pooled estimates, with uptake particularly weak among patients with solid tumors. The authors note that their retrospective, single-center design has limits, including incomplete medical records, unknown testing indications, and possible selection bias, and that treatment-related immunosuppression may have blunted antibody detectability in some patients. Still, the scale of the cohort and the length of the observation window lend weight to the conclusion. As vaccination coverage expands and screening becomes more systematic, the residual burden of HBV exposure among cancer patients should continue to shrink, provided that prevention reaches the demographic groups the data show are still being left behind. The research, conducted at the São Paulo State Cancer Institute, analyzed nearly 29,000 adult cancer patients treated between 2010 and 2023. International guidelines recommend HBV screening before chemotherapy, but implementation remains inconsistent. The findings highlight ongoing challenges in addressing HBV-related health inequities and the need for improved vaccination and diagnostic practices.

news.content: Biotechnology Epigenetic Editing Could Wipe Out Chronic Hepatitis B Infections An experimental therapy kept the virus at bay for at least six months. The approach could target other stubborn viruses too. Shelly Fan Oct 06, 2026 Image Credit Colorized models of hepatitis B viruses / NIAID on Unsplash Share Viruses are sneaky things. When they die, their DNA often sticks around. Some of them transform into freely roaming DNA that evades treatment. Others tunnel into their host’s genome and lie dormant, sometime for decades. But dormant doesn’t mean gone. When the time is right, they strike. If a patient with hepatitis B virus (HBV) or HIV stops taking antiviral drugs, it can trigger a severe rebound of the disease. Stress, aging , and other factors that dampen the immune system can also reactivate the chickenpox virus, triggering the painful, blistering rash known as shingles. Now, scientists have found a way to shut down one of these biological sleeper agents. Called epigenetic silencing , the technology hunts down lingering HBV genes in infected mice and adds a chemical tag that switches the genes off, without cutting the viral DNA. Unlike gene editing tools that shred genetic material, potentially causing collateral damage to the host’s genome, the epigenetic approach could be safer but still long-lasting. After three monthly doses, roughly 90 percent of the mice showed no signs of the virus for at least six months after their final shot. A safety test in monkeys found no notable side effects, including any signs of a runaway immune response. The team stopped short of calling it a cure. But if proven to be as helpful in humans, the injections could replace daily pills charged with keeping the virus in check and help millions of people laden with chronic hepatitis B. Earlier this year, the first patient was treated with the formulation in an ongoing Phase 1/2 clinical trial , which is testing for safety and early efficacy. If successful, the work could lead to treatments that silence the DNA of other viruses too. “This differentiated mechanism has the potential to enable durable antiviral control,” wrote the team at nChroma Bio, a biotechnology company based in Boston, and collaborators. Shape Shifter Chronic HBV infection is a silent killer. A person can feel totally healthy. Meanwhile, the virus repeatedly cycles between dormant and active states, triggering the immune system to attack infected cells in the liver. Over time , the repeated assaults leave scar tissue that slowly replaces the organ’s healthy architecture and causes it to malfunction. Even with its considerable regenerative capability, the liver struggles to do its usual work, from making enzymes that break down food to producing proteins that help blood clot. Blood pressure in the digestive system skyrockets, increasing the risk of deadly stomach bleeding. Even more insidious, the virus increases the risk of liver cancer, sometimes before notable tissue damage or symptoms. When HBV DNA integrates into the host’s genome, it can alter nearby gene activity, disrupt tumor-suppressing genes, or even rearrange chromosomes . Meanwhile, constant inflammation can further fuel the development of cancer. There are ways to fight back: Vaccines prevent infection, and antivirals suppress the virus. These drugs mimic the DNA letters HBV needs to replicate. Once incorporated into the viral genome, they block any further copying. But they’re a Band-Aid, not a cure. Stop taking them, and HBV rebounds in nearly everyone thanks to its two stubborn forms of DNA. One of these is called cccDNA, a tiny, chromosome-like structure that sits inside infected cells and acts as a reservoir for the virus. It’s “the driver of HBV persistence,” wrote the team. The other is viral DNA that has integrated into the host genome. These fragments continuously churn out viral proteins, which train the host’s immune system to recognize them as friendly. Whole viruses can then escape surveillance and continue replicating. “Thus, effective therapies for chronic hepatitis B must ultimately address both forms of viral DNA,” the team wrote. Easy Silence Previous methods have used various gene editors to hunt down and destroy viral DNA. In mice and monkeys, these tools have suppressed viral loads by up to 96 percent , with some effects lasting over a year. Be Part of the Future Sign up to receive top stories about groundbreaking technologies and visionary thinkers from SingularityHub. 100% Free. No Spam. Unsubscribe any time. The approach nChroma is developing, CRMA-1001, works differently. Rather than cutting viral DNA with the gene editor CRISPR-Cas9 or rewriting DNA with base editing, nChroma turned to epigenetics, the system of chemical tags that control whether genes are turned on or off. The new treatment mimics an epigenetic process for silencing genes called methylation. It combines genetic instructions to build a DNA methylation enzyme with a version of Cas9, stripped of its cutting ability. Here, Cas9 acts like a molecular docking system, while a guide RNA directs the machinery to a specific site in the HBV genome. All components are packaged into lipid nanoparticles. After injection into the bloodstream, they predominantly travel to the liver and methylate the viral DNA reservoir and integrated HBV DNA. In mice, a single dose slashed viral DNA activity and HBV surface protein levels more than a thousandfold. Among animals given three monthly doses, roughly 90 percent maintained undetectable viral load after six months. Adding standard antivirals to the mix lowered viral DNA levels even further. The team then tested escalating doses in cynomolgus monkeys for safety. At the highest dose, liver enzymes rose in the blood, suggesting the liver’s cells were stressed or injured. But the levels returned to normal within four weeks of the last dose. The animals didn’t show clinical symptoms of liver damage, such as anatomical changes or blood-clotting issues. The therapy has now entered the clinic . The team launched a trial in Hong Kong and received authorization to begin trials in New Zealand and the United Kingdom. They have competition too. In May, Seattle-based Tune Therapeutics reported early results from an ongoing phase 1/2 trial of its own epigenetic silencer. After a single dose, several HBV-associated biomarkers plummeted for at least 17 months, and none of the participants experienced severe side effects. In Shanghai, China, Epigenic Therapeutics is pursuing a similar strategy. Its formulation showed promise in preclinical models and is advancing toward a clinical trial , although details on how their silencer works are scant. How long the effects will last is an open question. Can patients eventually stop taking antivirals and be functionally cured? And whether the therapies can silence the full range of HBV variants, whose genomes can differ by more than eight percent , is also unknown. Then there’s the risk these therapies go rogue and methylate other parts of the host genome with unintended consequences. Costs could pose another challenge. Most people with chronic hepatitis B live in less economically developed regions in Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, where access to expensive, specialized treatments may be limited. Still, “epigenetic editing is an exciting, reversible solution that can long-term silence viral repertoires without the genotoxicity of gene editing,” wrote Marleen van der Laan at the University of Groningen and colleagues in an independent review. “Its success in functionally curing chronic hepatitis B is highly promising, but further steps are required to ensure its applicability.” Shelly Fan Shelly Fan Dr. Shelly Xuelai Fan is a neuroscientist-turned-science-writer. She's fascinated with research about the brain, AI, longevity, biotech, and especially their intersection. As a digital nomad, she enjoys exploring new cultures, local foods, and the great outdoors. Still, “epigenetic editing is an exciting, reversible solution that can long-term silence viral repertoires without the genotoxicity of gene editing,” wrote Marleen van der Laan at the University of Groningen and colleagues in an independent review. “Its success in functionally curing chronic hepatitis B is highly promising, but further steps are required to ensure its applicability.” Shelly Fan Shelly Fan Dr. Shelly Xuelai Fan is a neuroscientist-turned-science-writer. She's fascinated with research about the brain, AI, longevity, biotech, and especially their intersection. As a digital nomad, she enjoys exploring new cultures, local foods, and the great outdoors. analysis.brief_en: A groundbreaking study published in October 2026 by SingularityHub highlights a new epigenetic editing approach that could potentially eliminate chronic hepatitis B infections. The method, developed by nChroma Bio and collaborators, targets HBV DNA in infected mice and monkeys by adding chemical tags that switch the genes off without altering the viral DNA itself. After three monthly doses, approximately 90% of the mice showed no signs of the virus for at least six months, and safety tests in monkeys found no notable side effects. The treatment, called CRMA-1001, uses a modified version of the CRISPR-Cas9 system to deliver genetic instructions for DNA methylation, primarily targeting the liver. While the team did not call it a cure, the results suggest it could replace daily antiviral pills for chronic hepatitis B. The approach also has potential for treating other stubborn viruses. The first human patient was treated in an ongoing Phase 1/2 trial, and further research is needed to confirm its effectiveness in people. The method addresses both forms of HBV DNA—cccDNA and integrated DNA—which are known to evade treatment and contribute to liver damage and cancer risk.

news.title_zh: 表观遗传编辑可以消灭 慢性乙型肝炎 感染 - SingularityHub
news.source_body_en: A groundbreaking study published in October 2026 by SingularityHub highlights a new epigenetic editing approach that could potentially eliminate chronic hepatitis B infections. The method, developed by nChroma Bio and collaborators, targets HBV DNA in infected mice and monkeys by adding chemical tags that switch the genes off without altering the viral DNA itself. After three monthly doses, approximately 90% of the mice showed no signs of the virus for at least six months, and safety tests in monkeys found no notable side effects. The treatment, called CRMA-1001, uses a modified version of the CRISPR-Cas9 system to deliver genetic instructions for DNA methylation, primarily targeting the liver. While the team did not call it a cure, the results suggest it could replace daily antiviral pills for chronic hepatitis B. The approach also has potential for treating other stubborn viruses. The first human patient was treated in an ongoing Phase 1/2 trial, and further research is needed to confirm its effectiveness in people. The method addresses both forms of HBV DNA—cccDNA and integrated DNA—which are known to evade treatment and contribute to liver damage and cancer risk.
news.content_zh: SingularityHub 于 2026 年 10 月发表的一项开创性研究强调了一种新的表观遗传编辑方法,该方法有可能消除 慢性乙型肝炎 感染。该方法由 nChroma Bio 及其合作者开发,通过添加化学标签来关闭基因,而不改变病毒 DNA 本身,从而靶向感染小鼠和猴子中的 HBV DNA。三个月剂量后,大约 90% 的小鼠在至少六个月内没有表现出病毒迹象,并且对猴子的安全测试没有发现明显的副作用。治疗 称为 CRMA-1001,使用 CRISPR-Cas9 系统的修改版本来传递 DNA 甲基化的遗传指令,主要针对肝脏。虽然该团队并未称其为治愈方法,但结果表明它可以替代 慢性乙型肝炎 每日服用的 抗病毒药物 药丸。该方法还具有治疗其他顽固病毒的潜力。第一位人类患者正在正在进行的 1/2 期试验中接受治疗,需要进一步的研究来确认其对人类的有效性。该方法针对两种形式的 HBV DNA(共价闭合环状DNA 和整合 DNA),已知它们可以逃避 治疗 并导致肝损伤和癌症风险。

analysis.time: HHS launches new major vaccine injury initiative Stephanie Soucheray The initiative includes a new National Institutes of Health clinic for suspected vaccine-related injuries.
analysis.event: A Danish university has approved a CDC-funded study in African newborns, in which only half of babies will receive the hepatitis B vaccine. The study has been condemned as unethical.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers. It focuses on the ethical concerns of the vaccine study rather than the health impact or risk of hepatitis B virus.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Danish university has approved the study, but the ethical condemnation remains. The source_assessment indicates that the information is from a reputable media source, and the confidence level is moderate due to the lack of detailed health impact data.

analysis.brief_en: A Danish university has approved a CDC-funded study in African newborns, where only half of the babies will receive the hepatitis B vaccine. The study has been condemned as unethical, raising concerns about its methodology and ethical implications. However, the report does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers related to the hepatitis B virus. The approval of the study highlights ongoing debates about vaccine ethics and public health interventions, but the lack of detailed health impact data means the risk and scale of the virus's effects are not quantified. The source is a reputable media outlet, and the confidence level is moderate due to the absence of explicit health impact metrics.

news.content_zh: 丹麦一所大学批准了一项由 CDC 资助的非洲新生儿研究,其中只有一半的婴儿会感染乙型肝炎 疫苗。这项研究被谴责为不道德的,引发了人们对其方法和伦理影响的担忧。然而,该报告没有提供与 乙型肝炎病毒 相关的具体病例数、死亡数或暴露数量。该研究的批准凸显了有关 疫苗 伦理和公共卫生干预措施的持续争论,但缺乏详细的健康影响数据意味着该病毒影响的风险和规模无法量化。来源是一家信誉良好的媒体,由于缺乏明确的健康影响指标,置信度中等。

news.content: Skip to main content Main navigation Top stories Health Crime Politics Business Tech Culture Sports Weird 1-1-2 Top stories Health Crime Politics Business Tech Culture Sports Weird 1-1-2 Image A doctor is comforting her patient - Credit: royalty / DepositPhotos - License: DepositPhotos Health Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment National Institute for Public Health and the Environment National Institute of Public Health and the Environment Public Health and the Environment RIVM National Institute for Public Health and the Environment hepatitis B Hepatitis C » More tags « Less tags Share this article: Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window More testing needed to reduce hepatitis B and C infections, warns Health Institute Tuesday, 6 October 2026 - 21:10 The Netherlands must step up its fight against hepatitis B and C, experts at the National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) say. The health institute has drawn up a plan to further reduce the viral infections, calling for more testing of people from countries where hepatitis is relatively more common. That covers a large part of the world, from countries in Eastern Europe to Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. One option the experts cite is testing asylum seekers for hepatitis after they arrive in the Netherlands. This is similar to the policy regarding tuberculosis, as anyone from a country where the disease is widespread is routinely tested. Better record-keeping could also yield gains. The RIVM wants a central system in which diagnoses and treatments are recorded. “With this insight, weak spots in care can be identified and addressed more quickly,” the explanation says. The plan is part of an update to the National Hepatitis Plan released in 2016. Despite progress, not all of the goals set a decade ago have been met, in part because of “a lack of funding and the Covid-19 pandemic,” according to the report released Monday. Each year, 450 to 500 people die from the effects of hepatitis B and C. Thousands of people carry the virus for years without knowing it, because symptoms appear only later. In addition to migrants, men who have sex with men, people who use drugs, and people in detention face a higher risk. Young children in the Netherlands are vaccinated against hepatitis B. Vaccination is also possible later in life. Public information about that needs to improve, the experts say. There is no vaccine against hepatitis C. The disease can usually be treated effectively, but the infection must be detected first. Hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver that occurs in several forms. Infections often cause no symptoms. With hepatitis B and C, however, chronic infections can develop and lead to serious illness. There is a risk of cirrhosis of the liver, which in turn raises the chances of liver cancer. Other symptoms include fatigue, fever, muscle pain, loss of appetite, and jaundice, in which the skin and eyelids, among other body parts, turn yellow. analysis.brief_en: The RIVM, the Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, has warned that more testing is needed to reduce hepatitis B and C infections. The institute has proposed a plan to increase testing among people from countries where hepatitis is more common, such as Eastern Europe, Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. This approach is similar to the tuberculosis testing policy, where individuals from high-prevalence regions are routinely tested. The RIVM also emphasizes the importance of better record-keeping to identify and address weaknesses in the healthcare system. Despite progress, the report notes that not all goals set a decade ago have been met due to a lack of funding and the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic. Each year, 450 to 500 people die from hepatitis B and C, and thousands remain unaware of their infection for years. Chronic infections can lead to serious conditions like cirrhosis and liver cancer. The plan is part of an updated National Hepatitis Plan, and the RIVM is calling for improved public information about hepatitis B vaccination, which is already available for young children but could be expanded for adults.

Follow-Up Data of AHB-137 Treatment in Chronic Hepatitis B in Two Late-Breaking Oral Presentations at AASLD The Liver Meeting® 2026 News provided by AusperBio Therapeutics Inc. Oct 07, 2026, 20:30 ET Share this article Share toX Share this article Share toX Two abstracts on long-term follow-up data of AHB-137 treatment for chronic hepatitis B have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting® 2026. SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AusperBio Therapeutics, Inc. and Ausper Biopharma Co., Ltd. (together, "AusperBio"), a near-commercial biopharmaceutical company, today announced that two abstracts reporting long-term follow-up data of AHB-137 treatment have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting® 2026, the annual meeting of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD), to be held November 5–9 in Denver, Colorado, USA. The presentations will report long-term follow-up from the AB-10-8004 study (NCT07146100) in two populations of participants with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) who completed prior AHB-137 clinical studies: nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) treatment-experienced patients, and treatment-naïve patients who received AHB-137 monotherapy. "We are honored that two abstracts from the AB-10-8004 study have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting®," said Chris Yang, Co-founder and CSO of AusperBio. "We look forward to sharing these long-term follow-up data with the hepatology community as we continue to advance AHB-137 toward our goal of a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B." The presentation details are as follows: Publication Number: 5001 Abstract Title: Durability of AHB-137 up to 9 Month Post End-of-Studies in Nucleos(t)ide Analogue Treated Participants with Chronic Hepatitis B: First Long-Term Follow-up Report from the AB-10-8004 Study Session: Late Breaking Abstract Parallel Session Date and Time: November 8, 2026, 2:00 pm – 2:15 pm MT Presenter: Jinlin Hou, MD, Southern Medical University, Guangdong, China Publication Number: 5010 Abstract Title: Durability of Functional Cure to AHB-137 Monotherapy in Treatment-Naïve Participants with Chronic Hepatitis B: Long-Term Follow-Up Results of the AB-10-8004 Study Session: Late Breaking Abstract Parallel Session 2 Date and Time: November 8, 2026, 6:00 pm – 6:15 pm MT Presenter: Junqi Niu, MD, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China Late-breaking abstracts will be available on the AASLD website beginning at 8:00 am MT on November 5, 2026. AusperBio plans to issue a press release with additional details following the presentations. The full scientific program for The Liver Meeting® 2026, as well as the abstracts, can be found on the AASLD website. About AHB-137 AHB-137 is AusperBio's lead investigational unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy for chronic hepatitis B (CHB), developed using the Company's proprietary Med-OligoTM ASO platform. AHB-137 is designed to suppress hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) production, inhibit viral DNA replication, and promote immune reactivation, with the goal of achieving a functional cure for CHB. AHB-137 has demonstrated promising clinical results and is currently being evaluated in a Phase 3 trial in China, following completion of a global Phase 1 study and multiple Phase 2 studies. The Company is advancing AHB-137 through a coordinated global development strategy toward potential commercialization. AHB-137 is an investigational product candidate and has not been approved by any regulatory authority. About AusperBio AusperBio is a near-commercial biopharmaceutical company focused on developing differentiated oligonucleotide therapeutics and targeted delivery technologies, with an initial focus on achieving a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B. Follow-Up Data of AHB-137 Treatment in Chronic Hepatitis B in Two Late-Breaking Oral Presentations at AASLD The Liver Meeting® 2026 News provided by AusperBio Therapeutics Inc. Oct 07, 2026, 20:30 ET Share this article Share toX Share this article Share toX Two abstracts on long-term follow-up data of AHB-137 treatment for chronic hepatitis B have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting® 2026. SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AusperBio Therapeutics, Inc. and Ausper Biopharma Co., Ltd. (together, "AusperBio"), a near-commercial biopharmaceutical company, today announced that two abstracts reporting long-term follow-up data of AHB-137 treatment have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting® 2026, the annual meeting of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD), to be held November 5–9 in Denver, Colorado, USA. The presentations will report long-term follow-up from the AB-10-8004 study (NCT07146100) in two populations of participants with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) who completed prior AHB-137 clinical studies: nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) treatment-experienced patients, and treatment-naïve patients who received AHB-137 monotherapy. "We are honored that two abstracts from the AB-10-8004 study have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting®," said Chris Yang, Co-founder and CSO of AusperBio. "We look forward to sharing these long-term follow-up data with the hepatology community as we continue to advance AHB-137 toward our goal of a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B." The presentation details are as follows: Publication Number: 5001 Abstract Title: Durability of AHB-137 up to 9 Month Post End-of-Studies in Nucleos(t)ide Analogue Treated Participants with Chronic Hepatitis B: First Long-Term Follow-up Report from the AB-10-8004 Study Session: Late Breaking Abstract Parallel Session Date and Time: November 8, 2026, 2:00 pm – 2:15 pm MT Presenter: Jinlin Hou, MD, Southern Medical University, Guangdong, China Publication Number: 5010 Abstract Title: Durability of Functional Cure to AHB-137 Monotherapy in Treatment-Naïve Participants with Chronic Hepatitis B: Long-Term Follow-Up Results of the AB-10-8004 Study Session: Late Breaking Abstract Parallel Session 2 Date and Time: November 8, 2026, 6:00 pm – 6:15 pm MT Presenter: Junqi Niu, MD, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China Late-breaking abstracts will be available on the AASLD website beginning at 8:00 am MT on November 5, 2026. AusperBio plans to issue a press release with additional details following the presentations. The full scientific program for The Liver Meeting® 2026, as well as the abstracts, can be found on the AASLD website. About AHB-137 AHB-137 is AusperBio's lead investigational unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy for chronic hepatitis B (CHB), developed using the Company's proprietary Med-OligoTM ASO platform. AHB-137 is designed to suppress hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) production, inhibit viral DNA replication, and promote immune reactivation, with the goal of achieving a functional cure for CHB. AHB-137 has demonstrated promising clinical results and is currently being evaluated in a Phase 3 trial in China, following completion of a global Phase 1 study and multiple Phase 2 studies. The Company is advancing AHB-137 through a coordinated global development strategy toward potential commercialization. AHB-137 is an investigational product candidate and has not been approved by any regulatory authority. About AusperBio AusperBio is a near-commercial biopharmaceutical company focused on developing differentiated oligonucleotide therapeutics and targeted delivery technologies, with an initial focus on achieving a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B. The Company's innovation engine is built on its proprietary Med-OligoTM ASO and Au-HALOTM targeted delivery platforms, supporting the development of therapies across multiple oligonucleotide modalities. With multiple clinical-stage programs and a growing pipeline, AusperBio is advancing a backbone-based combination strategy for functional cure of CHB while exploring opportunities in additional disease areas with significant unmet medical needs.
