news.content: Yerevan 9 °C USD / AMD 361.97 English ArmeniaEconomyWorldCultureSportsFact CheckExclusive Projects ... PhotosVideos newsfeed Armenia12:50, 6 October 2026 WHO’s ETAGE validates Armenia as having reached regional hepatitis B control targets 8 minute read Armenia has been validated by the European Technical Advisory Group of Experts (ETAGE) as a country that has reached the regional targets for hepatitis B control through immunization. ETAGE is a body of 6–8 immunization experts appointed by the WHO Regional Director for Europe. This group is tasked with providing independent review and expert technical input to WHO/Europe’s vaccine-preventable diseases and immunization programme (VPI), with the goal of facilitating and accelerating achievements in relation to European Immunization Agenda 2030, including eradication, elimination and control of vaccine-preventable diseases in the WHO European Region. In connection with this achievement, an official certificate was presented to Armenia at the initiative of the World Health Organization (WHO) Country Office in Armenia. Within the framework of the assessment conducted by the World Health Organization, key factors included high vaccination coverage against hepatitis B, prevention of perinatal transmission, and ensuring a low prevalence of HBsAg among vaccinated groups. The achievement is an important step in Armenia’s immunization and hepatitis B prevention efforts and reflects the results of the consistent policies and measures implemented by the Government of the Republic of Armenia and the Ministry of Health. Minister of Health of the Republic of Armenia Anahit Avanesyan, welcoming those present at the ceremony, said that the certificate is a major achievement and testifies that the national immunization program is working and is already producing results. “Our children are free from acute hepatitis B and this very severe chronic disease. This is first and foremost a health issue, but it is also an economic issue. Every month, a person living with chronic hepatitis B spends 30,000-40,000 drams just on medication. Imagine what a huge burden this is for each person and family, as well as for the state. By investing in the health of our children, we are keeping them free from this disease and the costs associated with it in the future. I think this is a very significant result, and I congratulate and thank the entire healthcare system, our healthcare workers, healthcare organizers and the Ministry for this achievement,” the minister said. Avanesyan said that achieving good results does not mean stopping; it is necessary to move forward and set new targets. “Of course, this is an occasion to look back and see that our policies and efforts are producing results, and to move forward with the aim of embracing even greater targets. We are also now discussing the issue of providing medicines for the management of chronic hepatitis B, because it is very important that our patients are also protected in terms of their ongoing treatment. First of all, we plan to consider including pregnant women in this program, and later expanding it as well. But we must continue the very important work of vaccination and the overall immunization program. These achievements can be very easily lost; we must preserve them and improve them even further,” the minister said. Dr. Roberta Pastore, Lead for Immunization Programme Strengthening at the WHO Regional Office for Europe, emphasized that she was happy to be in Armenia and to represent the WHO Regional Office for Europe, noting that Armenia has achieved the hepatitis B control targets through vaccination. According to her, in 2015, within the framework of the European Vaccine Action Plan, the WHO Regional Office for Europe declared hepatitis B control a priority. It continues to remain a goal within the European Immunization Agenda 2030, as well as within regional action plans for the elimination of viral hepatitis. “The achievement of the hepatitis B control targets is confirmed through a rigorous assessment process, within which vaccination coverage indicators and the prevalence of hepatitis B are studied. Armenia has undertaken all the necessary steps to collect evidence confirming the achievement of the hepatitis B control targets. The validation process in Armenia confirmed that over the past two decades, the country’s efforts have been successful in introducing universal hepatitis B vaccination among newborns and children and ensuring high vaccination coverage,” Pastore said. According to her, this proves that Armenia has not only reached its hepatitis B control target, but has gone beyond it, moving closer to the goal of eliminating the disease. “I would like to congratulate you on this achievement, which makes Armenia one of 11 validated countries. Thanks to your commitment to and investment in vaccination over the past two decades, you have been able to create a generation of children and adolescents who will grow up to be healthier adults. They will be free from hepatitis B infection and its severe and fatal consequences,” she said. Dr. Stepan Atoyan, Director General of the National Center for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) of the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Armenia, speaking about the path to achieving the target, noted that this is not only a summary of the work done over the past years, but also a journey based on consistent state and healthcare policies, the dedicated work of healthcare professionals and the support of international partners. “We know that hepatitis B vaccination was introduced into the national immunization schedule about 30 years ago and, like any newly introduced vaccine, went through its subsequent stages: first rejection, then partial acceptance, and finally acceptance. As a result, we now have the picture that was mentioned by our colleague. Social studies that have been conducted also attest to this success. Acute hepatitis B is no longer being recorded among children, which speaks to the success of the vaccination process. At the same time, I would like to note that this certificate is, of course, very binding, because, as Ms. Avanesyan mentioned in her remarks, last year we recorded a fairly high rate among children under one year of age, and we are obliged to maintain this high rate and, naturally, preserve it,” Atoyan said. He also thanked the minister for her personal participation in the digitalization process, as the digitalization of healthcare services greatly contributes to the immunization process, as well as to epidemiological surveillance and disease control. news.content_zh: 经欧洲技术咨询专家组 (ETAGE) 确认,世界卫生组织 (WHO) 已确认亚美尼亚已通过其免疫计划达到了区域乙型肝炎控制目标。这一成就反映了亚美尼亚在过去二十年中一贯政策和措施的成功,包括在新生儿和儿童中普及乙型肝炎疫苗接种。验证过程涉及研究疫苗接种覆盖指标和乙型肝炎患病率,目的是减轻该疾病给个人和国家带来的负担。世界卫生组织欧洲区域办事处强调了严格的评估过程,而亚美尼亚卫生部长Anahit Avanesyan则指出,该证书是一个重要的里程碑,证明了国家免疫规划的有效性。她强调需要继续疫苗接种努力并设定新目标。亚美尼亚国家疾病控制和预防中心 (NCDC) 也对一致的国家和医疗保健政策、医疗保健专业人员的奉献以及国际合作伙伴的支持表示认可。这一成就被描述为免疫和乙型肝炎预防方面的重要一步,并计划在未来将该计划扩大到包括孕妇。

news.content: Skip to main content Main navigation News Antimicrobial Resistance COVID-19 Chronic Wasting Disease Influenza Public Health Alerts All Topics A-Z Coronavirus Vaccines Roadmap Influenza Vaccines Roadmap Roadmaps for Priority Pathogens Vaccine Integrity Project CIDRAP Leadership Forum . . Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Hepatitis B vaccine study condemned as unethical wins approval from Danish university Liz Szabo, MA Hepatitis Childhood Vaccines Tiago_Fernandez/iStock Share Copied to clipboard The University of Southern Denmark confirmed that it has given the green light to a controversial study in Guinea-Bissau, funded with $1.6 million from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), that plans to offer life-saving hepatitis B vaccines to only half of enrolled babies. News of the study, first reported in December by CIDRAP News, prompted an international outcry from health groups and political leaders, who condemned its design as unethical. Those concerns led Guinea-Bissau officials and administrators at the Danish university to place the study on hold for several months. Nearly one in five people in Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, which kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections by causing cancer or liver failure. Vaccinating babies at birth is safe and can prevent lifelong infections. Yesterday, citing unnamed sources, Rolling Stone broke the news that the Danish university had approved the clinical trial and that CDC leaders were pushing for the study to resume. The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, did not respond to questions before press time. The Danish researchers leading the study in Guinea-Bissau, Peter Aaby, PhD, and Christine Stabell Benn, MD, PhD, could not be reached for comment. In response to earlier criticism, their research group, the Bandim Health Project, defended their choice to withhold the birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine from half of the 14,000 newborns to be enrolled in the clinical trial. In a statement on Bandim’s website, researchers wrote, “No child enrolled in the study will receive fewer vaccines than under current national policy in Guinea-Bissau,” a developing country with far fewer resources than the United States and Europe. Guinea-Bissau does not currently vaccinate newborns against hepatitis B, as recommended by the World Health Organization, but plans to begin in 2028. University official cites revised study protocol An official at the University of Southern Denmark confirmed to CIDRAP News that he granted approval yesterday to proceed with the study, in spite of widespread ethical concerns. Professor Jakob Grauslund, PhD, MD, dean of the university’s faculty of health sciences, said he approved the study based on “an independent ethical assessment” carried out by the school’s research ethics committee. “The revised protocol also received ethical approval from the relevant ethics committee in Guinea-Bissau this summer,” Grausland said. “Final governmental authorization in Guinea-Bissau has, however, not yet been granted, and the study cannot begin until the necessary national authorization has been obtained.” An official from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) had little to say when asked about the study at a Thursday morning press conference. “There was ongoing discussions between the US government, who is supporting this research, and also the government” of Guinea-Bissau, said Wessam Mankoula, MD, a medical epidemiologist and acting director of Africa CDC’s Center of Public Health Emergency. “We can give you later updates about the most recent development as to the implementation of the study.” Stand Up for Science, a nonprofit advocacy group, vowed to stop the Danish study. “This is a gross violation of human rights and the use of bad science against some of the most vulnerable people in the world,” said Colette Delawalla, MD, the group’s founder and CEO, in a press release. analysis.time: The study was approved by the University of Southern Denmark in October 2026, with earlier concerns raised in December 2026. The study is set to resume after obtaining necessary national authorization in Guinea-Bissau, which has not yet been granted.
analysis.location_and_population: The study is taking place in Guinea-Bissau, a country with a high hepatitis B infection rate (nearly one in five people). The target population is newborns, with 14,000 enrolled babies.
analysis.event: A controversial hepatitis B vaccine study in Guinea-Bissau, funded by the CDC, was approved by the University of Southern Denmark despite ethical concerns. The study plans to offer the vaccine to only half of the enrolled babies, which has drawn international criticism.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Hepatitis B infection rates in Guinea-Bissau are high, with 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections dying from liver cancer or failure. The study's design has been condemned as unethical, leading to a temporary hold on the research.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was placed on hold for several months due to ethical concerns. The University of Southern Denmark has approved the study, but final governmental authorization in Guinea-Bissau has not been obtained. The Africa CDC is aware of the study but has not provided detailed comments.

analysis.brief_en: A controversial hepatitis B vaccine study in Guinea-Bissau, funded by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), has been approved by the University of Southern Denmark despite ethical concerns. The study, which plans to offer the vaccine to only half of the 14,000 enrolled newborns, has drawn international criticism for its design. The approval came after a revised protocol received ethical clearance from both the Danish university and Guinea-Bissau's ethics committee. However, the study cannot begin until final governmental authorization is obtained in Guinea-Bissau. The country has a high hepatitis B infection rate, with nearly one in five people infected, and 15% to 25% of those with chronic infections dying from liver cancer or failure. The study's ethical issues have led to a temporary hold, and the Africa CDC has not provided detailed comments. Advocacy groups have condemned the study as a violation of human rights and are exploring actions to prevent its implementation.

news.content_zh: 由美国疾病控制与预防中心 (CDC) 资助、在几内亚比绍进行的一项有争议的乙型肝炎 疫苗 研究,尽管存在伦理问题,但已获得南丹麦大学的批准。该研究计划仅向 14,000 名登记新生儿中的一半提供 疫苗,但其设计招致了国际批评。该批准是在修订后的方案获得丹麦大学和几内亚比绍道德委员会的道德许可后获得的。然而,在获得几内亚比绍政府的最终授权之前,研究无法开始。该国乙型肝炎感染率很高,近五分之一的感染者,15%至25%的慢性感染者死于肝癌或衰竭。该研究因伦理问题而被暂时搁置,非洲疾控中心尚未提供详细评论。倡导团体谴责这项研究侵犯人权,并正在探讨采取行动阻止其实施。

news.content: Overslaan en naar de inhoud gaan Direct naar de hoofdnavigatie Rijksinstituut voor Volksgezondheid en Milieu Ministerie van Volksgezondheid, Welzijn en Sport Nederlands English RIVM De zorg voor morgen begint vandaag Menu Home Onderwerpen Over RIVM Publicaties International Contact Agenda Mijn RIVM Nederlands English Zoekveld Zoeken Zoeken Rijksinstituut voor Volksgezondheid en Milieu Veel bezocht Coronaprik 2026 PFAS Gordelroosvaccinatie Actuele informatie Ebola Nieuws Suikerbelasting kan gelden voor ruim 40% van de suikers die mensen binnenkrijgen De overheid overweegt een suikerbelasting op etenswaren in te voeren. Het RIVM heeft twee opties voor deze suikerbelasting onderzocht. Een optie waarbij producten met minimaal 6 gram suiker per 100 gram (6%-variant) belast worden en een optie waarbij producten met minstens 20 gram suiker per 100 gram (20%-variant) belast worden. Het onderzoek laat zien welk deel van de suikers die mensen in Nederland binnenkrijgen dan belast worden. Opvoedprogramma positief voor gezondheid en bespaart zorgkosten Het RIVM heeft berekend wat de maatschappelijke kosten en baten zijn van een groepsprogramma voor opvoeders. Dit programma is bedoeld voor opvoeders waarvan hun kinderen (2-12 jaar) extra risico lopen op het ontwikkelen van een gedragsstoornis. Healthy Living Florida Sets October 8 Lake Mary Hearing on Dropping Chickenpox, Hepatitis B and Two Other School Vaccine Requirements Published Oct 02, 2026 9:50 PM EDT By Joseph James NIKOLAY DOYCHINOV | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket Developing Story Note: This report covers new developments involving Florida's proposed changes to school and child-care vaccine rules. Information may change as the Florida Department of Health releases additional findings. The newest information comes from a hearing notice the department published in the Florida Administrative Register on September 30, 2026, and was last checked on October 2, 2026. Florida parents now have a firm date to weigh in before the state decides whether children still need four vaccines to enroll in school or day care. The Florida Department of Health will hold a public hearing on October 8, 2026, from 9 a.m. to noon at the Orlando Marriott Lake Mary, according to a notice in the Florida Administrative Register. The hearing covers the department's plan to drop entry requirements for the chickenpox (varicella), hepatitis B, pneumococcal conjugate, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccines. The rule has not taken effect, and nothing about the recommended childhood vaccine schedule changes because of it. The vaccines would remain available, but schools, preschools, daycares, and adult education programs could no longer require proof of them, as WUSF reported. That puts the decision squarely on families, many of whom rely on enrollment paperwork as a reminder of which shots their child is due for. The stakes may be greatest for households with babies and toddlers in group care. Hib and pneumococcal vaccines are given mainly in the first years of life, when those infections are most dangerous, so a day-care classroom, not a high school hallway, is where the rule change could matter first. A Lake Mary Ballroom Becomes the Last Public Stop The hearing will take place in Grand Ballroom E, F, G, and H of the hotel at 1501 International Parkway in Lake Mary, north of Orlando. The notice says the session will end at noon or when the hearing concludes, whichever comes first. People can request an agenda from Tom Bendle of the department's Division of Disease Control at Thomas.Bendle@flhealth.gov or 850-245-4342. The rule at issue, 64D-3.046 of the Florida Administrative Code, sets immunization paperwork for public and private schools from preschool through grade 12 and for adult education classes. The department also posted a notice of change to the proposed rule on September 30, though its online summary does not describe the edits. MedicalDaily first reported in August that Florida moved to drop four school vaccine requirements after Surgeon General Dr. Joseph Ladapo approved the proposal. At that time, the plan was open for written comments, which the proposed rule notice said would run from August 24 to September 14. Earlier this week, MedicalDaily also covered a measles modeling study that projected outbreak risks if school coverage fell further. The new development is the in-person hearing, the only public hearing announced so far. Ladapo's Rationale Meets Pediatricians' Warnings In its proposed rule notice, the department said the change "removes from requirements immunizations that are not required by section 1003.22, Florida Statutes." In practice, the state is keeping only the shots that lawmakers wrote into law. The measles, mumps, rubella, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough requirements stay because only the Legislature can remove them. The same proposal would let parents cite moral and ethical beliefs on the state's religious exemption form. Ladapo has framed the effort as a matter of medical freedom and parental choice. At a September 3, 2025, news conference in Valrico, he said of vaccine mandates, "Every last one of them is wrong and drips with disdain and slavery," according to a PolitiFact review that rated the comparison Pants on Fire, its lowest rating. The Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics sees a different risk. "Even when exercised infrequently, nonmedical exemptions are neither harmless nor benign," the group said, adding that such exemptions "lead to lower immunization rates and weaken our ability as a state to protect ourselves against dangerous diseases." Doctors at a department workshop in December 2025 also raised concerns about meningitis, WUSF reported. Day-Care Families Face the First Practical Questions Florida's vaccine coverage has already slipped. Vaccination rates among the state's children have fallen nearly 5% since the 2019-20 school year, and only 88.8% of kindergartners had the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine in 2024-25, according to WUSF. That is below the national average of 93% and short of the 95% level linked to preventing measles outbreaks. Those numbers concern a vaccine that is not part of this rule, but they show the trend pediatricians fear could spread to the four shots now under review. Hib can cause meningitis, pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and throat swelling, mainly in children under 5, according to the CDC. The agency recommends the vaccine for all children in that age group. Children too young to finish their shots, and those with weakened immune systems, depend most on high coverage among classmates. Parents can take simple steps now. They can ask their pediatrician or county health department for their child's record and confirm whether any doses are overdue, since doctor recommendations have not changed. Families can also ask their day care or school how it will respond, since the proposal removes requirements but does not stop programs from encouraging vaccination. Cost should not be a barrier for many households. Most private insurance plans cover routine childhood vaccines, and the federal Vaccines for Children program supplies them at no cost to eligible children through county health departments and participating clinics. Parents with questions about a specific vaccine or their child's health should talk with a clinician. Adoption Timeline Remains Unsettled The department has not announced when it will file the rule for adoption, and no effective date has been set. Under Florida's rulemaking process, a rule generally takes effect 20 days after it is filed with the Department of State unless a later date is listed. It remains unclear whether the notice of change will alter the final version or whether a legal challenge will follow. MedicalDaily will track the hearing and any filing that follows. For now, the four vaccines remain required for Florida school and day-care entry, and doctors still recommend them on the usual schedule. Families who want a voice in the decision have one week to plan, and checking a child's vaccine record is a reasonable step whatever the outcome. Read more Kentucky's Measles Count More Than Doubles Since Mid-August to 46 with Four Hospitalized and No Recorded Vaccinations Liberals and Conservatives Each Doubted the Other Side's Religious Exemption Claims in a New Behavioral Science Study Pediatricians Widen the RSV High Risk List and More Toddlers Now Qualify for a Second Season Dose Key Questions Answered When and where is Florida's vaccine rule hearing? The Florida Department of Health will hold the hearing on October 8, 2026, from 9 a.m. to noon at the Orlando Marriott Lake Mary, 1501 International Parkway. It may end earlier if the hearing concludes before noon. Which vaccines would no longer be required? The proposal would remove school and child-care entry requirements for the chickenpox, hepatitis B, pneumococcal conjugate, and Hib vaccines. These shots would still be available and recommended by doctors. Are measles and polio shots still required in Florida schools? Yes. Measles, mumps, rubella, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough requirements are written into state law, so only the Florida Legislature can change them. Has the rule already taken effect? No. The hearing is still ahead, the department has not filed the rule for adoption, and no effective date has been announced. The four vaccines remain required for now. Who could be most affected if the rule is adopted? Infants and toddlers in day care face the greatest exposure risk, because Hib and pneumococcal infections are most dangerous in children under 5. Children with weakened immune systems and those too young to finish their vaccine series also rely on high coverage around them. What can parents do right now? Parents can review their child's vaccine record with a pediatrician or county health department, ask their school or day care how it plans to respond, and attend the hearing or contact the department to share their views. Those numbers concern a vaccine that is not part of this rule, but they show the trend pediatricians fear could spread to the four shots now under review. Hib can cause meningitis, pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and throat swelling, mainly in children under 5, according to the CDC. The agency recommends the vaccine for all children in that age group. Children too young to finish their shots, and those with weakened immune systems, depend most on high coverage among classmates. Parents can take simple steps now. They can ask their pediatrician or county health department for their child's record and confirm whether any doses are overdue, since doctor recommendations have not changed. Families can also ask their day care or school how it will respond, since the proposal removes requirements but does not stop programs from encouraging vaccination. Cost should not be a barrier for many households. Most private insurance plans cover routine childhood vaccines, and the federal Vaccines for Children program supplies them at no cost to eligible children through county health departments and participating clinics. Parents with questions about a specific vaccine or their child's health should talk with a clinician. Adoption Timeline Remains Unsettled The department has not announced when it will file the rule for adoption, and no effective date has been set. Under Florida's rulemaking process, a rule generally takes effect 20 days after it is filed with the Department of State unless a later date is listed. It remains unclear whether the notice of change will alter the final version or whether a legal challenge will follow. MedicalDaily will track the hearing and any filing that follows. For now, the four vaccines remain required for Florida school and day-care entry, and doctors still recommend them on the usual schedule. Families who want a voice in the decision have one week to plan, and checking a child's vaccine record is a reasonable step whatever the outcome. Read more Kentucky's Measles Count More Than Doubles Since Mid-August to 46 with Four Hospitalized and No Recorded Vaccinations Liberals and Conservatives Each Doubted the Other Side's Religious Exemption Claims in a New Behavioral Science Study Pediatricians Widen the RSV High Risk List and More Toddlers Now Qualify for a Second Season Dose Key Questions Answered When and where is Florida's vaccine rule hearing? The Florida Department of Health will hold the hearing on October 8, 2026, from 9 a.m. to noon at the Orlando Marriott Lake Mary, 1501 International Parkway. It may end earlier if the hearing concludes before noon. Which vaccines would no longer be required? The proposal would remove school and child-care entry requirements for the chickenpox, hepatitis B, pneumococcal conjugate, and Hib vaccines. These shots would still be available and recommended by doctors. Are measles and polio shots still required in Florida schools? Yes. Measles, mumps, rubella, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough requirements are written into state law, so only the Florida Legislature can change them. Has the rule already taken effect? No. The hearing is still ahead, the department has not filed the rule for adoption, and no effective date has been announced. The four vaccines remain required for now. Who could be most affected if the rule is adopted? Infants and toddlers in day care face the greatest exposure risk, because Hib and pneumococcal infections are most dangerous in children under 5. Children with weakened immune systems and those too young to finish their vaccine series also rely on high coverage around them. What can parents do right now? Parents can review their child's vaccine record with a pediatrician or county health department, ask their school or day care how it plans to respond, and attend the hearing or contact the department to share their views. news.source_body_en: Florida is set to hold a public hearing on October 8, 2026, in Lake Mary to discuss the potential removal of school vaccine requirements for chickenpox, hepatitis B, and two other vaccines. The hearing notice was published in the Florida Administrative Register on September 30, 2026, and the event is part of an ongoing review of vaccine mandates. The Florida Department of Health has not confirmed or denied the status of hepatitis B virus in the evidence provided. The hearing aims to gather public input from parents regarding the proposed changes, which could affect children enrolled in school or day care. No confirmed cases, deaths, or exposures related to hepatitis B virus are reported in the evidence. The hearing is a consultation process and does not provide definitive conclusions about the virus's impact or status.
news.content_zh: 佛罗里达州定于 2026 年 10 月 8 日在玛丽湖举行公开听证会,讨论可能取消学校对水痘、乙型肝炎和其他两种 疫苗 的 疫苗 要求。听证会通知于 2026 年 9 月 30 日在佛罗里达州行政登记册上发布,该活动是对 疫苗 指令正在进行的审查的一部分。佛罗里达州卫生部尚未在提供的证据中确认或否认 乙型肝炎病毒 的状态。听证会旨在收集家长对拟议变更的公众意见,这可能会影响就读学校或日托机构的儿童。证据中没有报告与 乙型肝炎病毒 相关的确诊病例、死亡或暴露情况。听证会是一个咨询过程,不会提供有关病毒影响或状况的明确结论。

Food Triggers in IBD — News and commentary from the world of gastroenterology and hepatology by Ian Ingram, Managing Editor, MedPage Today October 8, 2026 • 2 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday In a large Korean cohort, accelerated biological aging was associated with a 93% increased risk of early-onset colorectal adenocarcinoma and a 132% higher risk of early-onset colon adenocarcinoma specifically. (Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology) An algorithm using routinely collected clinical parameters could offer insight into pancreatic cancer risk in type 2 diabetes patients, a study from China suggested. (Gut) Experts in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology reviewed the diagnosis and management of acid-related disorders, including gastroesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcer disease, and more. Anorectal biofeedback therapy and dextranomer-hyaluronate injections showed similar efficacy in a randomized study of refractory fecal incontinence. (Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology) Researchers suggested there's a marginal risk of hepatitis B virus transmission from domestic cats to humans. (Hepatology) In a phase II trial of chronic hepatitis C, an 8-week course of investigational bemnifosbuvir and ruzasvir led to sustained virologic response in 90% of patients at 12 weeks. (Hepatology) The American College of Gastroenterology issued new guidelines on preventive care in cirrhosis. (American Journal of Gastroenterology) Renin-angiotensin system inhibitors and calcium channel blockers may be liver protective for hypertensive patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. (Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology) Resmetirom's (Rezdiffra) efficacy in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) appeared to be independent of common MASH risk genotypes, according to an analysis of the drug's pivotal trial. (Journal of Hepatology) Liver transplant for patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure was associated with markedly lower 1-year mortality in a global study. (Journal of Hepatology) Sex differences in hepatocellular carcinoma mortality. (JAMA Network Open) Why do inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients experience symptoms from foods they previously tolerated? Researchers uncovered clues. (Gastroenterology) Mount Sinai announced NIH funding for a study to investigate whether per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances -- so-called forever chemicals -- play a role in IBD development. In a nationwide cohort study, early surgical intervention with colectomy in ulcerative colitis was linked with lower cardiometabolic disease risks later on. (American Journal of Gastroenterology) A network meta-analysis of advanced therapies as induction for ulcerative colitis backed upadacitinib (Rinvoq) for efficacy and anti-p19 biologics in terms of safety. (Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology) Meanwhile, a retrospective study comparing JAK inhibitors for acute severe ulcerative colitis found a higher rate of colectomy at 52 weeks with Tofacitinib (Xeljanz) than with upadacitinib (42.5% vs 23.4%). supplementary_news.content: 40% of Liver Transplant Recipients Remain Unvaccinated Against Hepatitis B, Raising Risk of Severe Complications: Study A study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases found that only 60% of liver transplant recipients were vaccinated against hepatitis B virus (HBV), leaving 4 in 10 unprotected against potentially severe complications. Researchers from Baylor College of Medicine analyzed data from deceased-donor liver transplant recipients between September 2022 and June 2024 using the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database. Factors associated with lower vaccine uptake included older age, alcohol-associated liver disease, shorter waiting-list duration, and lower educational attainment. The findings highlight gaps in HBV vaccination coverage among liver transplant recipients and the need to improve pre-transplant vaccination practices. The study was conducted by Michael A. and colleagues. To estimate the viral hepatitis vaccination coverage rates at the national level and the clinicodemographic characteristics associated with lack of vaccination, scientists from the Baylor College of Medicine carried out a retrospective cohort study based on the analysis of national registry data. Researchers obtained data from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry that included all adults who received liver transplantation from a deceased donor within September 1, 2022, and June 30, 2024. The research team studied immunization history, region, cause of liver disease, waitlist time, age, and socioeconomic status of patients. Key findings: - Results from the data analysis from the United Network for Organ Sharing database for the period of 22 months showed large gaps in vaccination, along with clear demographic differences. - Less than 59.9% of patients who had received liver transplants using deceased donor organs from September 1, 2022, to June 30, 2024, had been fully immunized for the hepatitis B virus. - This means that about 40% of patients were not vaccinated prior to transplantation. Immunity levels varied geographically throughout transplant regions of the country. - Vaccination levels were independently linked to advanced age and low educational level of the patients. - The presence of alcohol-related liver disease and short waiting list times were also independent predictors of vaccination. In summary, empirical data from the UNOS registry highlight important gaps in pre-transplant preventive care in terms of lack of protection against hepatitis B virus among 40 percent of patients receiving livers. The findings of the study clearly indicate the importance of implementing multilevel interventions along with new vaccines to ensure the immunization of high-risk populations. Reference: Michael A Shi, Jeong Han, Ramsey Albahra, Maria F Machicao, Chia-Yu Chiu, Saira Khaderi, Ruben Hernaez, Fasiha Kanwal, Hashem B El-Serag, George Cholankeril, Tzu-Hao Lee, Hepatitis B Vaccination for Liver Transplant Recipients in the United States: A National Cohort Study, Clinical Infectious Diseases, 2026;, ciag585, https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciag585 Dr Riya Dave has completed dentistry from Gujarat University in 2022. She is a dentist and accomplished medical and scientific writer known for her commitment to bridging the gap between clinical expertise and accessible healthcare information. She has been actively involved in writing blogs related to health and wellness. Dr Kamal Kant Kohli-MBBS, DTCD- a chest specialist with more than 30 years of practice and a flair for writing clinical articles, Dr Kamal Kant Kohli joined Medical Dialogues as a Chief Editor of Medical News. Besides writing articles, as an editor, he proofreads and verifies all the medical content published on Medical Dialogues including those coming from journals, studies,medical conferences,guidelines etc. Email: drkohli@medicaldialogues.in. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 7, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer Hepatitis B exposure declines among cancer patients, yet disparities persist by October 7, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Hepatitis B exposure declines among cancer patients, yet disparities persist Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Hepatitis B virus remains one of the most consequential viral pathogens in oncology, and a new fourteen-year analysis from Brazil shows that while exposure to the virus is steadily falling among people with cancer, it is far from disappearing. Researchers at the University of São Paulo examined nearly 29,000 adult cancer patients treated at a major quaternary oncology center between 2010 and 2023 and found that the proportion carrying antibodies indicating past or present HBV infection dropped from 16.5 percent to 9.9 percent over the study period. The decline, reported in the journal Cancer Causes & Control, is encouraging evidence that vaccination and changing screening practices are reshaping the viral landscape faced by oncologists. Yet the same data reveal stubborn gaps: men, older adults, and non-White patients continue to bear a disproportionate burden of previous HBV exposure, and a substantial share of admitted cancer patients were never tested at all. The clinical stakes of this epidemiology are considerable. Hepatitis B virus infects hepatocytes and can establish a chronic infection that progresses to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; infection is recognized as one of the strongest risk factors for liver cancer, raising the odds of that malignancy by roughly 47-fold. Globally, an estimated 240 million people live with chronic HBV infection. For cancer patients, the virus carries an additional threat: systemic anticancer therapies suppress immune function, which can permit viral replication to resume even in patients whose infection appeared resolved. This reactivation is driven by covalently closed circular DNA, a persistent viral reservoir that remains within the nucleus of hepatocytes long after serological recovery. A recent global meta-analysis estimated reactivation rates of approximately 10 percent among patients with hematological malignancies and 5 percent among those with solid tumors. Reactivation is not a benign event. It can force interruption, delay, or modification of cancer treatment precisely when therapy is most needed, and it may culminate in acute hepatitis, liver failure, and death. For this reason, international guidelines recommend screening for HBV before patients begin chemotherapy or other immunosuppressive regimens. Patients who test positive for the hepatitis B surface antigen should receive antiviral therapy with agents such as entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, or tenofovir alafenamide, while those who are surface-antigen negative but positive for antibody against the core antigen, known as anti-HBc, should be considered at risk of reactivation and managed with antiviral prophylaxis or serological and molecular monitoring. Despite these recommendations, screening remains inconsistently implemented across oncology centers worldwide. The São Paulo study drew on laboratory records from the São Paulo State Cancer Institute, affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the university’s Faculty of Medicine, which has treated more than 140,000 cancer patients since opening in 2008. Of 125,985 patients admitted between 2010 and 2023, 28,869, or 22.9 percent, underwent anti-HBc testing. The mean age of those tested was 56 years, roughly two-thirds were women, and 61.4 percent self-identified as White. Solid tumors accounted for 71.2 percent of the cohort, with breast cancer the most common diagnosis, while hematological malignancies made up 22.2 percent, led by non-Hodgkin lymphoma and multiple myeloma. HBV exposure was defined as anti-HBc positivity, a marker that indicates prior contact with the virus but does not by itself distinguish resolved infection from active disease. The headline finding is a statistically significant downward trend in seroprevalence, from 16.5 percent in 2010 to 9.9 percent in 2023. The decline was broad but uneven. Among men, seroprevalence fell from 25.1 percent to 12.3 percent, a steeper drop than among women, whose rates fell from 11.4 percent to 8.3 percent. Every age group improved, including patients aged 18 to 39, whose seroprevalence fell from 7.7 percent to 2.4 percent, and those aged 60 and older, whose rates declined from 20.1 percent to 13.7 percent. Seroprevalence also fell significantly among White patients and among those with solid tumors. By contrast, no significant trend emerged among non-White individuals, whose rates moved only from 21.4 percent to 17.7 percent, or among patients with hematological malignancies, whose rates remained essentially flat at around 13 percent. Multivariable logistic regression sharpened the demographic picture. Patients aged 60 or older had 4.4-fold higher odds of HBV exposure than those under 40, men had 89 percent higher odds than women, and non-White patients had 25 percent higher odds than White patients. The age gradient likely reflects cumulative lifetime exposure in cohorts born before universal neonatal vaccination, compounded by the reduced immunogenicity of hepatitis B vaccines in older adults. The sex difference may have biological underpinnings: androgens exert immunosuppressive effects, while estrogens appear to enhance immune and vaccine responses, potentially leaving men less able to clear or control the virus. The ethnic disparity points toward inequities in social determinants of health, including unequal access to vaccination, diagnosis, and treatment, a pattern consistent with prior Brazilian and international studies. Cancer type itself was not independently associated with exposure, but subgroup patterns were striking. Among hematological malignancies, non-Hodgkin lymphoma showed a seroprevalence of 15.5 percent, a malignancy repeatedly linked to HBV in meta-analyses, though the mechanisms remain unresolved. Among solid tumors, the highest rates appeared in sarcoma, at 43.5 percent, a figure the authors caution may be inflated by small numbers, and in liver and bile duct cancers, at 31.2 percent. In adjusted analyses, liver and bile duct cancers carried more than threefold higher odds of HBV exposure, and gastrointestinal cancers carried 41 percent higher odds, findings consistent with the established oncogenic role of the virus, which operates through chronic hepatic inflammation, integration of viral DNA into the host genome, and the activity of viral proteins such as HBx. Within the anti-HBc-positive group, additional testing of subsets clarified the virological picture. The hepatitis B surface antigen was positive in 7.8 percent of those tested, indicating current infection, while 73.2 percent carried anti-HBs antibodies consistent with resolved infection. Among 484 patients who underwent HBV DNA testing, 25.6 percent had detectable viral load. Taken together, most anti-HBc-positive patients showed evidence of past exposure, but a meaningful minority carried molecular or serological signs of active infection, underscoring why confirmatory testing matters before immunosuppressive therapy begins. One encouraging operational trend accompanied the epidemiological one: the proportion of admitted patients screened for anti-HBc rose from 11.1 percent in 2010 to 29.2 percent in 2023. Even so, more than two-thirds of cancer patients admitted over the period were never tested, and global data suggest screening before chemotherapy reached only about 57 percent in pooled estimates, with uptake particularly weak among patients with solid tumors. The authors note that their retrospective, single-center design has limits, including incomplete medical records, unknown testing indications, and possible selection bias, and that treatment-related immunosuppression may have blunted antibody detectability in some patients. Still, the scale of the cohort and the length of the observation window lend weight to the conclusion. As vaccination coverage expands and screening becomes more systematic, the residual burden of HBV exposure among cancer patients should continue to shrink, provided that prevention reaches the demographic groups the data show are still being left behind. AusperBio to Present Long-Term Follow-Up Data of AHB-137 Treatment in Chronic Hepatitis B in Two Late-Breaking Oral Presentations at AASLD The Liver Meeting® 2026 PR Newswire Wed, October 7, 2026 at 8:30 PM EDT 4 min read Two abstracts on long-term follow-up data of AHB-137 treatment for chronic hepatitis B have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting® 2026. SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AusperBio Therapeutics, Inc. and Ausper Biopharma Co., Ltd. (together, "AusperBio"), a near-commercial biopharmaceutical company, today announced that two abstracts reporting long-term follow-up data of AHB-137 treatment have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting® 2026, the annual meeting of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD), to be held November 5–9 in Denver, Colorado, USA. AusperBio The presentations will report long-term follow-up from the AB-10-8004 study (NCT07146100) in two populations of participants with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) who completed prior AHB-137 clinical studies: nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) treatment-experienced patients, and treatment-naïve patients who received AHB-137 monotherapy. "We are honored that two abstracts from the AB-10-8004 study have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting®," said Chris Yang, Co-founder and CSO of AusperBio. "We look forward to sharing these long-term follow-up data with the hepatology community as we continue to advance AHB-137 toward our goal of a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B." The presentation details are as follows: Publication Number: 5001 Abstract Title: Durability of AHB-137 up to 9 Month Post End-of-Studies in Nucleos(t)ide Analogue Treated Participants with Chronic Hepatitis B: First Long-Term Follow-up Report from the AB-10-8004 Study Session: Late Breaking Abstract Parallel Session Date and Time: November 8, 2026, 2:00 pm – 2:15 pm MT Presenter: Jinlin Hou, MD, Southern Medical University, Guangdong, China Publication Number: 5010 Abstract Title: Durability of Functional Cure to AHB-137 Monotherapy in Treatment-Naïve Participants with Chronic Hepatitis B: Long-Term Follow-Up Results of the AB-10-8004 Study Session: Late Breaking Abstract Parallel Session 2 Date and Time: November 8, 2026, 6:00 pm – 6:15 pm MT Presenter: Junqi Niu, MD, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China Late-breaking abstracts will be available on the AASLD website beginning at 8:00 am MT on November 5, 2026. AusperBio plans to issue a press release with additional details following the presentations. The full scientific program for The Liver Meeting® 2026, as well as the abstracts, can be found on the AASLD website. Story Continues About AHB-137 AHB-137 is AusperBio's lead investigational unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy for chronic hepatitis B (CHB), developed using the Company's proprietary Med-OligoTM ASO platform. AHB-137 is designed to suppress hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) production, inhibit viral DNA replication, and promote immune reactivation, with the goal of achieving a functional cure for CHB. AHB-137 has demonstrated promising clinical results and is currently being evaluated in a Phase 3 trial in China, following completion of a global Phase 1 study and multiple Phase 2 studies. The Company is advancing AHB-137 through a coordinated global development strategy toward potential commercialization. AHB-137 is an investigational product candidate and has not been approved by any regulatory authority. About AusperBio AusperBio is a near-commercial biopharmaceutical company focused on developing differentiated oligonucleotide therapeutics and targeted delivery technologies, with an initial focus on achieving a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B. The Company's innovation engine is built on its proprietary Med-OligoTM ASO and Au-HALOTM targeted delivery platforms, supporting the development of therapies across multiple oligonucleotide modalities. With multiple clinical-stage programs and a growing pipeline, AusperBio is advancing a backbone-based combination strategy for functional cure of CHB while exploring opportunities in additional disease areas with significant unmet medical needs. B, Raising Risk of Severe Complications: Study Written By : Dr Riya Dave ,Medically Reviewed By : Dr. Kamal Kant Kohli Published On 2026-10-04T20:45:11+05:30 | Updated On 4 Oct 2026 8:45 PM IST A study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases found that only 60% of liver transplant recipients were vaccinated against hepatitis B virus (HBV), leaving 4 in 10 unprotected against potentially severe complications. Researchers from Baylor College of Medicine analyzed data from deceased-donor liver transplant recipients between September 2022 and June 2024 using the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database. Factors associated with lower vaccine uptake included older age, alcohol-associated liver disease, shorter waiting-list duration, and lower educational attainment. The findings highlight gaps in HBV vaccination coverage among liver transplant recipients and the need to improve pre-transplant vaccination practices. The study was conducted by Michael A. and colleagues. To estimate the viral hepatitis vaccination coverage rates at the national level and the clinicodemographic characteristics associated with lack of vaccination, scientists from the Baylor College of Medicine carried out a retrospective cohort study based on the analysis of national registry data. Researchers obtained data from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry that included all adults who received liver transplantation from a deceased donor within September 1, 2022, and June 30, 2024. The research team studied immunization history, region, cause of liver disease, waitlist time, age, and socioeconomic status of patients. Key findings: Results from the data analysis from the United Network for Organ Sharing database for the period of 22 months showed large gaps in vaccination, along with clear demographic differences. Less than 59.9% of patients who had received liver transplants using deceased donor organs from September 1, 2022, to June 30, 2024, had been fully immunized for the hepatitis B virus. This means that about 40% of patients were not vaccinated prior to transplantation. Immunity levels varied geographically throughout transplant regions of the country. Vaccination levels were independently linked to advanced age and low educational level of the patients. The presence of alcohol-related liver disease and short waiting list times were also independent predictors of vaccination. In summary, empirical data from the UNOS registry highlight important gaps in pre-transplant preventive care in terms of lack of protection against hepatitis B virus among 40 percent of patients receiving livers. The findings of the study clearly indicate the importance of implementing multilevel interventions along with new vaccines to ensure the immunization of high-risk populations. supplementary_news.content: HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Screening to Begin in Govt De-addiction Facilities Yudh Nashean Virudh is leading revolution towards a stronger, healthier and prosperous Punjab: Dr. Balbir Singh. Published on: Oct 5, 2026, 11:15:35 IST By Genesis Prefer HT on Google Share via Copy link Punjab’s fight against drug abuse and communicable diseases is strengthening with Triple H screening for HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C set to begin shortly in government de-addiction and rehabilitation facilities. Punjab launches triple H screening to combat drug abuse and infectious diseases. The decision is part of the Bhagwant Mann's Yudh Nashean Virudh initiative and aims to provide comprehensive treatment to people with substance-use disorders and prevent the spread of blood-borne infections in the state. Viral infections like HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C spread through risk behaviors like sharing needles and syringes, and detecting and treating these diseases is an important part towards reintegrating people suffering from addiction back in their communities. For years, screening camps for HIV and hepatitis were organised periodically, often at intervals of about two months. While these camps provided opportunities for testing, there was limited scope to track who had attended, who had missed the camp and who subsequently required follow-up. Under the new approach, screening will be linked directly to the de-addiction and rehabilitation process rather than relying primarily on periodic camps. This is expected to create more consistent opportunities for testing and facilitate referrals for individuals who require further investigation, treatment or continued medical care. Health and Family Welfare Minister Dr Balbir Singh said, “People with a history of injecting drug use face an increased risk of blood-borne infections, and that early detection is important for timely medical care and counselling.” He added, “Under the leadership of Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann, Yudh Nashean Virudh is leading a revolution towards a stronger, healthier and prosperous Punjab. Our goal is not simply to help people overcome addiction, but also to enable them to lead healthier lives and contribute to society. By integrating HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C screening into de-addiction services, the Government is taking another important step towards ensuring that recovery leads to a meaningful and brighter future.” Earlier, a person who missed a screening camp could remain outside the testing cycle until another camp was held weeks or months later. By linking testing with de-addiction services, the state can easily identify those who need to be screened and ensure that positive cases are referred for appropriate care. The decision reflects the state’s seriousness in battling the spread of infectious diseases in the state. Earlier in August, Dr. Balbir Singh announced adoption of advanced testing technologies, including Nucleic Acid Testing (NAT) and Chemiluminescence Immunoassay (CLIA), to enhance the early detection of transfusion-transmitted infections such as HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C and strengthen blood safety in Punjab. Diagnostic testing for the three infections can also be availed free-of-cost at all Aam Aadmi Clinics in the state. These infections can remain undetected for years because many infected individuals do not experience noticeable symptoms, even as the underlying disease progresses. Early diagnosis and treatment, however, can improve treatment outcomes and help patients to live long, healthy lives. The integration of Triple H screening also reflects a broader approach to substance-use treatment, recognising that recovery goes beyond withdrawal management and abstinence. Counselling, psychological support, medical care and social rehabilitation are all important components of sustained recovery, alongside the identification and management of associated health conditions. With the rollout already underway in private facilities and government centres expected to follow shortly, the initiative seeks to strengthen the continuum of care available to people affected by substance use. supplementary_news.content: Press Releases Precision BioSciences Announces Late-Breaking Oral Presentation for PBGENE-HBV at AASLD The Liver Meeting 2026 October 8, 2026 | 9 min read Twitter LinkedIn Facebook Email Print DURHAM, N.C.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Precision BioSciences, Inc. (Nasdaq: DTIL), a clinical stage gene editing company utilizing its novel proprietary ARCUS® platform to develop in vivo gene editing therapies for high unmet need diseases, today announced that it has been selected to deliver a late-breaking oral presentation at The Liver Meeting 2026, the 77 th annual meeting of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD). The Liver Meeting 2026 will take place November 5-9 in Denver, CO. Details of the oral presentation: Type of presentation: Late-breaking oral presentation Abstract title: Durable pgRNA loss in both HBeAg positive and negative patients treated with PBGENE-HBV supports path towards viral cure Presenter: Man-Fung Yuen Authors: Man-Fung Yuen, Anca Streinu Cercel, Vlad A. Ichim, Emily B. Harrison, James M. Harris, Keely Dulmage, Andrew Van Cott, Abhishek Chandiramani, Neil Leatherbury, Janel Lape, Peter Balfe, Jeff Smith, Cassandra L. Gorsuch, Stanley Frankel, Oby Sogbetun, Jane McKeating, Mark S. Sulkowski, Edward J. Gane Date and time: Sunday, November 8, 2026, 2:15PM-2:30PM MST Publication number: 5002 About PBGENE-HBV (Hepatitis B Viral Elimination Program): PBGENE-HBV is Precision’s wholly owned in vivo gene editing program being evaluated in ELIMINATE-B, a global clinical trial, as a potential curative treatment for chronic hepatitis B. PBGENE-HBV is the only clinical stage program that targets and eliminates covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), the sole source of viral replication, leading to sustained loss of pregenomic RNA (pgRNA), the precursor for HBV DNA. PBGENE-HBV is the first and only in vivo gene elimination approach to prospectively employ repeat lipid nanoparticle (LNP) administration in chronic hepatitis B with the goal of viral cure, as measured by sustained undetectable HBV DNA off nucleos(t)ide therapy. The FDA has previously provided guidance that undetectable HBV DNA is a validated endpoint for chronic hepatitis B. PBGENE-HBV has been granted Fast Track designation by the FDA. Further details on the trial can be found on Precision’s website and on clinicaltrials.gov under identifier NCT06680232. About Hepatitis B: Chronic hepatitis B viral (HBV) infection causes inflammation and damage to the liver, leading to increased risk of death from liver cancer or cirrhosis. There is no cure for chronic hepatitis B, and current treatments rarely result in a functional cure, primarily due to persistence of viral DNA in the liver. In patients with chronic hepatitis B, cccDNA, which contains the full-length viral genome, persists long term, produces pgRNA, and is the sole source of new infectious viral particles. Since cccDNA is the only source of infectious particles (HBV DNA), we believe elimination of cccDNA could result in a viral cure of chronic hepatitis B. Sustained loss of HBV DNA alone as a result of cccDNA elimination is a validated endpoint for the FDA and highly relevant for PBGENE-HBV. About the ELIMINATE-B Trial: The Phase 1 ELIMINATE-B study is currently enrolling both HBeAg negative and positive chronic hepatitis B patients at world-class sites in the United States, Europe, Asia and Oceania. The goal of the study is to define the optimal dose and number of dose administrations for safely eliminating cccDNA. Precision continues to accelerate recruitment and evaluate a genetically diverse patient population in the Phase 1 study. About Precision BioSciences, Inc. Precision BioSciences, Inc. is a clinical stage gene editing company dedicated to improving life (DTIL) with its novel and proprietary ARCUS ® genome editing platform that differs from other technologies in the way it cuts, its smaller size, and its simpler structure. These features are intended for ARCUS nucleases to drive more defined therapeutic outcomes. Using ARCUS, the Company’s pipeline is comprised of clinical stage in vivo gene editing candidates designed to deliver lasting cures for the broadest range of genetic and infectious diseases where no adequate treatments exist. For more information about Precision BioSciences, please visit www.precisionbiosciences.com . The ARCUS ® platform is being used to develop in vivo gene editing therapies for sophisticated gene edits, including gene elimination (removing a viral genome e.g. viral DNA such as in the Company’s PBGENE-HBV program), and excision (removing a large portion of a defective gene by delivering two ARCUS nucleases in a single AAV such as in the Company’s PBGENE-DMD program) and gene insertion (inserting DNA into a gene to cause expression or add function). supplementary_news.content: Manila Bulletin Opinion Vaccine-preventable cancers Opinion Vaccine-preventable cancers By Raymundo W. Lo, MD, FPSP UNDER THE MICROSCOPE You read that right. Apart from vaccines treating and curing cancers, they can actually prevent cancers! There are many viruses/bacteria that are known to cause cancer, either because they hijack the cell’s mechanisms for repairing cell damage, which then goes on to cause genetic mutations that cause cancer, or the organisms themselves are oncogenic, meaning they can cause cancers to develop. A study by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) in 2024 showed that one in eight cancers worldwide are believed to be caused by infections. That’s about 2.3 million (12 percent) of new cancer cases each year. That’s the same fraction as lung cancer in all cancers in the USA alone. Some cancer researchers believe the IARC’s estimate to be very conservative. What are these organisms and what cancers do they cause? The highest number of cancers caused by infections is gastric cancer, and the trigger is Helicobacter pylori infection. Almost 800,000 cases of gastric cancer occur annually. Though there are no vaccines yet for H. pylori, it can be detected by gastroscopy and treated with antibiotics. It is followed by the Human Papilloma Virus (HPV), which causes 750,000 cervical, anal, vulvar, penile cancers as well as head and neck cancers worldwide. Next is hepatitis B virus which is linked to around 360,000 cases of liver cancer worldwide, with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) responsible for 260,000 cases globally, mainly nasopharyngeal cancer, some gastric cancers, and Hodgkins lymphoma. Hepatitis C virus was responsible for 160,000 liver cancer cases worldwide. HIV is another virus that can cause cancers, due to the profound immunosuppression it causes. Typical tumors include Kaposi sarcoma, anal cancer, lung cancer, non-Hodgkins lymphoma, liver cancer, cervical cancer and head and neck cancers. Fortunately, new medications can now reduce HIV viral loads to zero, thus reducing the possibility of developing these cancers. The higher burden of infection-caused cancer cases is in the less-developed countries in Eastern Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Central and Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia. Here in the Philippines, we have high rates of infection for hepatitis B virus. The figures I gathered in the 1990s showed about 75 percent of Filipinos had been exposed to HBV with 15-20 percent carrier status, meaning they were living with HBV in their bodies and had a high risk of developing liver cancer, which is very deadly. Early vaccination of babies decreased hepatitis B carriers (0.8 percent among five to six year-olds in 2018) compared to 16.7 percent among adults in the pre-vaccination era. But liver cancer is still the fourth most common cancer type and the second most common cause of cancer deaths. Taiwan used to have many liver cancers but the incidence has dropped due to a very successful early HBV vaccination program. We also have high rates of cervical and nasopharyngeal cancers locally due to HPV, and now we have effective vaccines for this virus. The DOH has a campaign to vaccinate 12-year-old females against HPV but we have yet to see the results. It should also be given to young boys as they can infect the girls via sexual intercourse and both sexes can develop nasopharyngeal and other HPV-associated cancers. My column, “A new approach to cervical cancer screening” (March 12, 2024) proposed a viable path toward more women to be screened for HPV and early cervical cancer. Now, we have many effective tools for these infections, including vaccination (HBV and HPV), testing (H. pylori, HPV, HCV, HBV, HIV) screening, diagnosis and treatment of these cancer-causing infections. The key challenges are limited access to and uptake of these measures due to financial constraints and lack of political commitment. Social stigma related to infections (HIV, HPV) also play a role in preventing access to interventions. The IARC scientists said governments should prioritize scaling up these interventions to prevent transmission of these infections and prevent many infection-caused cancers. Top priority goes to highly effective vaccines and screening and treatment of persistent infections. So, why are vaccines taking the limelight now even as anti-vaxxer sentiment is on the rise worldwide? It’s because vaccines are highly effective in preventing infections for which vaccines are available. They act much in the same way the body responds to infections, which is to stimulate our immune systems to rev up our immune defenses against invaders. Now, vaccines are being employed to combat cancers, which are actually our own cells gone rogue. Most cancers have genetic mutations that set them apart from benign cells, and these mutations tend to evade the immune system. Cancer vaccines help our immune systems recognize the cancer cells and kill them. With the advent of immunotherapy for cancers, we are now making great strides in controlling a once formidable enemy. Vaccines against infections that cause cancers, and now directly against cancers are here to stay. It’s the wave of the future. Hear that, anti-vaxxers? close Manila Bulletin Weather Producer-20261008-09:04 CANCEL NEXT VIDEO play_arrow volume_mute AD % buffered 00:00 00:00 00:38 Powered by GliaStudios

supplementary_news.content: Home News Trending Celebrity Biography History Beauty Fashion Health Fitness Living Food Moms How Tos Money Business Career Opportunities Shop Fabwoman Amazon Store Product Reviews Relationships Marriage Weddings Insights From HPV to Hepatitis: 5 Infections That Can Increase Your Risk Of Cancer October 8, 2026Posted byby Anu Do you know that infections are the leading cause of cancer? Cancer, as we all know, has become a very common health issue, with millions of new cases springing up every day globally. According to a new study published in the journal The Lancet Oncology, about 1 in 8 cancer cases around the world may be linked to infections, many of which can be prevented through vaccines, screening, or straightforward treatments. The study also found that about 2.3 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, which is equivalent to 12% of all cancer diagnoses. The five leading infections were human papillomavirus (HPV), Helicobacter pylori, hepatitis B, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and hepatitis C. 1. Human papillomavirus (HPV) Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common sexually transmitted infection spread through intimate skin-to-skin contact, including vaginal, anal, or oral sex. It can spread even when an infected person has no visible signs or symptoms. Condoms can reduce the risk of transmission but do not provide complete protection because HPV can infect areas of skin that are not covered by a condom. According to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), HPV was responsible for approximately 750,000 cancer cases globally in 2024, making it one of the world’s leading infection-related causes of cancer. About 600,000 of these cases were cervical cancers. Vaccination is one of the most effective ways to prevent HPV-related cancers, while regular cervical cancer screening and checkups remain important. 2. Helicobacter pylori (H.pylori) Helicobacter pylori, commonly called H. pylori, is a bacterium that infects the stomach. H. pylori is a bacterial infection that infects the stomach and is a major cause of stomach issues such as ulcers and gastritis. It is usually spread through saliva, vomit, or stool. Chronic H. pylori infection can lead to inflammation and damage the stomach lining, increasing the risk of stomach (gastric) cancer. It is also associated with a type of lymphoma called MALT lymphoma. 760,000 new cancer cases in 2024 were attributable to H. pylori, according to IARC, making it the largest infection-related cause of cancer globally. Most of these cancers were stomach cancers. H. pylori infection can be treated with antibiotics, which can significantly reduce the risk of stomach cancer. 3. Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) Hepatitis B (HBV) is a virus that infects the liver and, if infection becomes chronic, it can cause inflammation and damage that may eventually lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer. It usually spreads when a person comes into contact with infected blood or certain body fluids. The latest IARC analysis estimates that HBV was responsible for approximately 360,000 cases of liver cancer globally in 2024. Because hepatitis B often causes no symptoms, infected people may not know they have it; therefore, vaccination offers the best protection. 4. Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a common virus estimated to infect about 95% of the world’s population and usually causes no serious long-term problems. While most people infected with EBV never develop cancer, the virus is associated with several cancers, including Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and most recently stomach cancers. IARC’s latest estimates put the number of EBV-attributable cancer cases at approximately 260,000 worldwide in 2024, making it the fourth-largest infectious cause of cancer globally. There is currently no licensed vaccine for the treatment of EBV. 5. Hepatitis C (HCV) Similar to Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C (HCV) is a virus that primarily attacks the liver. If untreated, chronic hepatitis C can cause liver inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, leading to an increase in the risk of liver cancer. HCV is also associated with some cases of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. IARC estimates that approximately 160,000 new cancer cases globally in 2024 were attributable to hepatitis C. Unlike hepatitis B, there is currently no vaccine for hepatitis C. However, a short course of antiviral drugs can cure more than 95% of infections and substantially reduce people’s risk of developing liver cancer. About the ELIMINATE-B Trial: The Phase 1 ELIMINATE-B study is currently enrolling both HBeAg negative and positive chronic hepatitis B patients at world-class sites in the United States, Europe, Asia and Oceania. The goal of the study is to define the optimal dose and number of dose administrations for safely eliminating cccDNA. Precision continues to accelerate recruitment and evaluate a genetically diverse patient population in the Phase 1 study. About Precision BioSciences, Inc. Precision BioSciences, Inc. is a clinical stage gene editing company dedicated to improving life (DTIL) with its novel and proprietary ARCUS® genome editing platform that differs from other technologies in the way it cuts, its smaller size, and its simpler structure. These features are intended for ARCUS nucleases to drive more defined therapeutic outcomes. Using ARCUS, the Company's pipeline is comprised of clinical stage in vivo gene editing candidates designed to deliver lasting cures for the broadest range of genetic and infectious diseases where no adequate treatments exist. For more information about Precision BioSciences, please visit www.precisionbiosciences.com. The ARCUS® platform is being used to develop in vivo gene editing therapies for sophisticated gene edits, including gene elimination (removing a viral genome e.g. viral DNA such as in the Company's PBGENE-HBV program), and excision (removing a large portion of a defective gene by delivering two ARCUS nucleases in a single AAV such as in the Company's PBGENE-DMD program) and gene insertion (inserting DNA into a gene to cause expression or add function).
