By Folasade Akpan An estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases globally in 2024 were attributable to infections, accounting for about 12 per cent of all new cancer cases, a study published in The Lancet Oncology has found. The study, titled “Global Burden of Cancer Attributable to Infections in 2024: A Worldwide Incidence Analysis”, provided an updated assessment of cancers linked to infectious agents. Discover more Cancer cancers cancer Led by researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the study used data from the Global Cancer Observatory’s GLOBOCAN 2024 database. It assessed cancers attributable to 12 infectious agents classified as Group 1 carcinogens by the IARC Monographs Programme. The researchers estimated population-attributable fractions, absolute numbers and age-standardised incidence rates by sex, age and country. They found that Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) accounted for the largest number of infection-attributable cancer cases, with about 760,000 cases globally. Human papillomavirus (HPV) followed with about 750,000 cases, while hepatitis B virus (HBV) was linked to 360,000 cases. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) accounted for about 260,000 cases, while hepatitis C virus (HCV) was associated with approximately 160,000 cases. The five infections accounted for the majority of cancers attributable to infectious agents in the study. The researchers said the findings underscored the importance of infection control in cancer prevention, noting that several of the infections could be prevented or treated. They identified interventions including HPV and HBV vaccination, testing and treatment for HIV, H. pylori, HBV and HCV, as well as safe injection practices. Other measures include condom use and pre-exposure prophylaxis to prevent HIV transmission, alongside screening for precancerous lesions linked to HPV-driven cervical and anal cancers. The study found that eastern Asia recorded the largest absolute burden, with about 990,000 infection-attributable cancer cases, representing 42 per cent of the global total. Sub-Saharan Africa, however, recorded an age-standardised incidence rate of 28.5 cases per 100,000 people, higher than the global average of 22.7 cases per 100,000. Central and eastern Europe recorded 24.3 cases per 100,000, while southeastern Asia recorded 23.1 cases per 100,000. Discover more Book a Checkup Nigerian News Subscription PM News ePaper The researchers said the analysis incorporated newly established infection-cancer associations and additional infectious agents, including HIV and Merkel cell polyomavirus. It also included additional cancer types associated with previously established carcinogenic infections, including the recently established link between EBV and gastric cancer. A focused analysis of EBV-attributable cancers also showed substantial regional differences in the distribution of cancer types associated with the virus. The researchers said the findings could inform research and development investments in new cancer prevention tools, especially those targeting EBV. They said strengthening vaccination, screening, diagnosis and treatment programmes could help reduce the global burden of cancers associated with infectious agents. The study noted that infectious agents remained an important preventable cause of cancer globally, making infection control a key component of broader cancer-control strategies. MEDINDIA MEDINDIA Consult Online Doctor Courses Explore Healthy Living News Health A-Z Calculators Articles Drugs Directories Education More Search Medindia Medindia » News » Health Watch » Can Infections Cause Cancer? 1 in 8 Cases Linked Can Infections Cause Cancer? 1 in 8 Cases Linked Written by Dr. Ankita Balar Arya Medically Reviewed by Colleen Fleiss M.Sc on Oct 5 2026 10:14 AM Listen to this article 0:00/0:00 1x 1.5x 2x Infections can cause some cancers. Learn how HPV, H. pylori and hepatitis viruses raise cancer risk and how prevention can help. Explore Interactive Learning: Infections Linked to Cancer Highlights: 2.3 million infection-related cancer cases were estimated worldwide in 2024 H. pylori and HPV accounted for about 760,000 and 750,000 cases 12 infectious agents were included in the global cancer analysis Can infections cause cancer? Yes, some can. In 2024, about 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide were estimated to be attributable to infections, equal to about 12% of all new cancer cases. That is roughly 1 in every 8 cancer cases. The finding comes from a worldwide incidence analysis that used global cancer data to estimate the share of cancer attributable to 12 infectious agents (1✔). This matters because some of these infection-related cancer risks are preventable. Vaccination, cancer screening, infection testing and appropriate treatment can reduce the risk of certain cancers. The key is understanding which infections are linked to cancer and which prevention measures are supported by evidence. Lifetime Risk Calculator for Cancers What are your chances for developing some common cancers in your lifetime - find out now. Which Infections Cause Cancer? The strongest cancer links in the 2026 analysis involved H. pylori, HPV, hepatitis B virus, Epstein-Barr virus and hepatitis C virus. Together, these infections accounted for most of the estimated infection-attributable cancer burden (1✔). H. pylori was associated with approximately 760,000 cancer cases in 2024. HPV followed with about 750,000 cases. Hepatitis B virus was linked to around 360,000 cases, Epstein-Barr virus to about 260,000, and hepatitis C virus to approximately 160,000 (1✔). These infections do not all cause the same cancers. H. pylori is strongly associated with stomach cancer. Persistent high-risk HPV infection is the main cause of cervical cancer. Hepatitis B and C are important causes of liver cancer, while Epstein-Barr virus is associated with several cancers (1✔). Tap to explore Which infections are linked to which cancers? Not all infections carry the same cancer risk. Tap each card to see the important connection. H. pylori Stomach infection ⌄ Main cancer link: Stomach cancer. Long-term H. pylori infection can cause persistent inflammation in the stomach lining and is an established cancer risk. HPV Human papillomavirus ⌄ Main cancer link: Cervical cancer. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types can cause abnormal cell changes that may progress to cancer. Hepatitis B & C Liver infections ⌄ Main cancer link: Liver cancer. Long-term hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection can cause chronic liver inflammation and damage, increasing liver cancer risk. Epstein-Barr virus A common virus ⌄ Main cancer links: Several cancers, including some lymphomas and nasopharyngeal cancer. The virus is also associated with some stomach cancers. An important distinction Infection does not equal cancer ⌄ What it means: Having one of these infections does not mean a person will develop cancer. Cancer risk depends on the infection and other biological and environmental factors. The key takeaway Some infection-related cancer risks can be reduced through prevention, screening, testing and appropriate treatment. Source: Research cited in this MedIndia News Human Papillomavirus Infection - Risk Factors, Symptoms, Screening, Treatment & Prevention Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, depending on the human papillomavirus that causes it, can result in common warts or can cause cervical cancer. How Do Infections Increase Cancer Risk? An infection can contribute to cancer through different biological processes. Some infections persist in the body for years and can cause ongoing inflammation or changes in cells. H. pylori can cause long-term inflammation in the stomach lining. Research also suggests that treating H. pylori infection can reduce the risk of gastric cancer. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis included 11 randomized controlled trials and found a lower risk of gastric cancer among H. pylori-positive people who received eradication therapy . HPV can cause abnormal cell changes when a high-risk infection persists. These changes may progress to cervical cancer over time. IARC reports that more than 99% of cervical cancer cases are caused by infection with HPV. Hepatitis B and hepatitis C can cause chronic inflammation and liver damage, increasing the risk of liver cancer. Epstein-Barr virus is associated with several cancers, including some lymphomas and nasopharyngeal cancer. The 2026 analysis also incorporated evidence linking Epstein-Barr virus with stomach cancer (3✔). Cervical Cancer - Types, Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment, Complications & Prevention Cancer cervix refers to cancerous growth in the cervix and usually occurs in the transition called squamo-columnar junction. How Many Cancer Cases Are Linked to Infections Worldwide? The 2026 analysis estimated that 2.3 million cancer cases were attributable to infections worldwide in 2024. The largest regional burden was in Eastern Asia, with approximately 990,000 cases, accounting for 42% of the global total (4✔). The study also found that infection-attributable cancer incidence was higher than the global average in sub-Saharan Africa, Central and Eastern Europe, and Southeast Asia. These differences reflect variation in infection prevalence and the availability of prevention, screening, diagnosis and treatment (1✔). The finding is not entirely new. Earlier IARC research using GLOBOCAN 2018 data estimated 2.2 million infection-attributable cancer cases worldwide. H. pylori, HPV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C were also among the leading contributors in that analysis (2✔). Liver Cancer - Types, Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Treatment, Prevention, Progosis Liver or hepatic cancer is an abnormal growth of cells in the liver. The leading cause of the disease is cirrhosis or scarring of the liver tissue. Can Cancer From Infections Be Prevented? Yes, some infection-related cancers can be prevented or their risk reduced. The approach depends on the infection. HPV vaccination can prevent infection with cancer-causing HPV types. Cervical screening can identify abnormal or precancerous changes before they develop into invasive cancer. Hepatitis B vaccination can prevent chronic hepatitis B infection, which is an important risk factor for liver cancer. Appropriate testing and treatment of H. pylori, hepatitis B and hepatitis C can also form part of cancer-prevention strategies (1✔). What Should You Do to Lower Your Infection-Related Cancer Risk? What you can do Why it matters Ask about recommended HPV vaccination HPV vaccination helps prevent infection with cancer-causing HPV types and can reduce the risk of HPV-related cancers (1✔). Follow recommended cervical screening Screening can detect HPV-related precancerous changes before they become cervical cancer (1✔). Check whether hepatitis B vaccination is appropriate Preventing hepatitis B infection can reduce the risk of hepatitis B-related liver cancer (1✔). Seek appropriate testing for persistent infections Identifying and treating infections such as H. pylori, hepatitis B and hepatitis C can help reduce infection-related cancer risk (1✔)(3✔). Do not assume an infection means you will get cancer Infection is one factor in cancer development. Individual risk depends on the infection and other biological and environmental factors (1✔)(2✔). The 2026 study was a population-level incidence analysis, not a clinical trial involving individual patients. Researchers used GLOBOCAN 2024 cancer incidence data and calculated population-attributable fractions for 12 infectious agents classified as Group 1 carcinogens by the IARC Monographs Programme. There was therefore no conventional patient sample size (1✔). This distinction is important. The estimate does not mean that doctors can look at an individual cancer diagnosis and conclude that an infection caused it simply because that infection is associated with the cancer. It describes the estimated burden across populations. The researchers also reported no funding for the study (1✔). The overall message is encouraging: some infection-related cancer risks can be addressed before cancer develops. Vaccination, appropriate screening and timely testing or treatment of relevant infections give people practical ways to reduce preventable cancer risks. Knowing these links turns a complex global cancer statistic into useful knowledge for everyday health decisions. Frequently Asked Questions Q: Can infections cause cancer? A: Yes. Certain infections are established causes of specific cancers, including infections involving HPV, H. pylori, hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus. Q: Which infections are linked to cancer? A: Important cancer-linked infections include HPV, H. pylori, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus and Epstein-Barr virus. Q: What percentage of cancers are caused by infections? A: About 12% of new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were estimated to be attributable to infections, equal to roughly 1 in 8 cases. Q: Can HPV cause cancer? A: Yes. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types can cause cervical cancer and is also associated with several other cancers. Q: How can infection-related cancer be prevented? A: Depending on the infection, prevention can include vaccination, cancer screening, appropriate infection testing and treatment, and safer infection-control practices. This is a gross violation of human rights and the use of bad science against some of the most vulnerable people in the world.” — Dr. Colette Delawalla, Founder and CEO of Stand Up for Science WASHINGTON, DC, UNITED STATES, October 8, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Following reports that the CDC intends to move forward with a previously-canceled study of the Hepatitis B vaccine in newborns in Guinea-Bissau, Stand Up for Science Founder and CEO Dr. Colette Delawalla released the following statement: “Not on our watch. We stopped this unethical study the first time and we’ll do it again. These are innocent babies and the last thing they need is RFK, Jr. doing another of his pet project experiments on them in pursuit of ‘evidence’ to support his dangerous anti-vax beliefs. This is a gross violation of human rights and the use of bad science against some of the most vulnerable people in the world.” First announced in late 2025, the U.S. taxpayer-funded trial intended to study whether the dose of Hepatitis B vaccine given to infants at birth had any potential negative health effects, despite the fact that the birth-dose vaccine has been used safely for decades. In January of this year, Stand Up for Science sent an on-the-ground investigator to Guinea-Bissau to learn more about the study. The trial was cancelled after the investigation and expert analysis found the study protocol contained major ethical issues, including the withholding of a proven intervention. This is not the first instance of Kennedy’s involvement with controversial anti-vax efforts on children in underdeveloped nations. In 2019, his efforts to discourage the measles vaccine in Samoa as then-chairman of the anti-vaccine nonprofit Children’s Health Defense was ultimately followed by an outbreak of thousands of measles cases, including deaths of children. Stand Up for Science is exploring all possible actions at its disposal to prevent this study from happening. Delawalla is available for comment and media appearances. ### Stand Up for Science is a grassroots, Washington, D.C. based, non-profit organization mobilizing the fight for science and democracy. Stand Up for Science was formed in February 2025 in response to actions affecting federal science agencies and funding of the American scientific ecosystem. On March 7th, Stand Up for Science mobilized over 50,000 people at 170+ events across the world on its first National Day of Action. Federal scientists across multiple agencies (NIH, EPA, NASA, FEMA) have chosen Stand Up for Science as the platform to publish their open letters of concern. DTIL, US74019P2074 Precision BioSciences announces HBV talk: Precision BioSciences stock gains 1.79 percent Published on 10/08/2026 at 16:25 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS Precision BioSciences stock costs EUR 5.68 on October 8, 2026. That is plus 1.79 percent versus EUR 5.58, with HBV data on November 8, 2026. Key points in brief Precision BioSciences announced a late-breaking PBGENE-HBV presentation at AASLD on October 8, 2026. The company reported 16 patients treated across 38 administrations in its hepatitis B program. The Lang & Schwarz price was EUR 5.68 on October 8, 2026, plus 1.79 percent versus EUR 5.58. DTIL, US74019P2074, Illustration mit AI erstellt. Precision BioSciences (ISIN US74019P2074) was trading at EUR 5.68 at Lang & Schwarz on October 8, 2026 at 4:11 p.m. CEST, up 1.79 percent versus EUR 5.58. According to Precision BioSciences on October 8, 2026, the company had been selected for a late-breaking oral presentation on PBGENE-HBV at The Liver Meeting 2026. release] Mirum Pharmaceuticals announces primary endpoint met in Phase 3 AZURE-1 study of brelovitug in chronic hepatitis delta virus Back to the "HIV and Co-Infections News" list Hepatitis October 3, 2026 Tags: Hepatitis D Share: Mirum Pharmaceuticals press release Mirum Pharmaceuticals, Inc. announced the primary endpoint was met in the Phase 3 portion of the AZURE-1 study evaluating brelovitug, an investigational fully human monoclonal antibody that binds to hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), for the treatment of chronic hepatitis delta virus (HDV). In addition, 48-week data from the Phase 2b portion of AZURE-1 demonstrated deepening viral suppression, with a greater proportion of patients achieving HDV RNA below the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ, <10 IU/mL) and target not detected (TND), and increased rates of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) normalization. AZURE-1 is one of two pivotal Phase 3 studies intended to form the basis of Mirum’s U.S. registration package for brelovitug. Read the full press release here. Florida to hear public input today on proposal to drop four school vaccine requirements WBBH US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 1:19 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 1:09 PM EDT Oct 8, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jackie Guenther Reporter Florida to hear public input Thursday on proposal to drop four school vaccine requirements The proposal would make the chickenpox, hepatitis B, pneumococcal and Hib vaccines optional for school and daycare entry. Updated: 1:09 PM EDT Oct 8, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jackie Guenther Reporter , Fla. — Florida health officials held a public hearing Thursday on a proposal that would remove school and daycare requirements for four vaccines. The vaccines under consideration protect against chickenpox, hepatitis B, pneumococcal disease and Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib. The Florida Department of Health’s proposal would remove the requirement for children to receive those shots to attend school or daycare. Advertisement The proposal has drawn concern from pediatricians, who warn that removing vaccine requirements could leave more children vulnerable to preventable diseases. The Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics has opposed the change. The proposal has not taken effect. The four vaccines remain required for school and daycare entry for now, and requirements for other vaccines, including measles and polio, would remain in place The hearing took place at 9 a.m. at the Orlando Marriott Lake Mary, north of Orlando.
